articles.title: GOP lawmakers pump brakes on Trump's $5K check promise: 'Where are you getting the money?'
articles.excerpt:
Several House Republicans spoke with Fox News Digital about President Donald Trump's promise of $5,000 checks for every adult American if the GOP wins in the midterms.

President Donald Trump's promis...
articles.body_text:
Several House Republicans spoke with Fox News Digital about President Donald Trump's promise of $5,000 checks for every adult American if the GOP wins in the midterms.

President Donald Trump's promise of a big payout for Americans if Republicans win the midterms is getting a rocky reception on Capitol Hill.

Several Republicans outright oppose the $5,000 check promise, while others offered tacit support in comments to Fox News Digital but hesitated on whether it could actually be delivered. It's a sign that the GOP will have an uphill fight to get the "Trump dividend" approved by Congress — with the president and lawmakers divided over whether it even needs the legislative branch's green light.

"I disagree with it. It's pay-to-play," Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., told Fox News Digital. "You shouldn't pay anybody to vote your conscience. Plus, where are you getting the money? I think we're in debt $40 trillion."

House Appropriations Committee Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., whose powerful committee would likely play a major role in crafting the $5,000 stimulus if it did run through Congress, said he was "skeptical" it could be achieved.

TRUMP FACES RECKONING AS GOP FIGURES LABEL $5K PROMISE A 'SOCIALIST VOTE-BUYING SCHEME'

President Donald Trump's $5,000 dividend promise could face resistance on Capitol Hill. (Getty Images/Fox News Digital illustration)

"Take a billion dollars ... I'd rather use it to either bolster defense or save Social Security. I think that's a better use of the money. But again, we have to see what we're looking at. Right now, we don't have a bill," Cole told Fox News Digital.

TRUMP DANGLES $5,000 CHECKS AS DEBT SURGES — BUT ONLY IF GOP CAN CLEAR MAJOR MIDTERM HURDLE

He added more optimistically, "We just have an idea that we want to get money back to the American people. I like that."

Rep. John Rutherford, R-Fla., said he could support the idea if the sudden injection of cash wouldn't send inflation rates soaring.

"But it ought to be limited — people that are working, people that are paying taxes. I don't think we should just send paychecks out to everybody willy-nilly," Rutherford told Fox News Digital.

Rep. Beth Van Duyne, R-Texas, simply said, "The devil's always in the details. I prefer to look at ways of getting people job opportunities."

Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., speaks to the media as he departs a House Republican conference meeting in the basement of the U.S. Capitol on Sept. 1, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

VOTERS HAVE A BLUNT MESSAGE FOR TRUMP ABOUT HIS IDEA TO DOLE OUT $5,000 CHECKS

Rep. Brad Knott, R-N.C., praised Trump's candor but signaled he was not enthusiastic about a stimulus without guardrails.

"If we can structure tax incentives, if we can do some type of — whether it's a cut, whether it's a rebate, something in that vein, I think it's probably a little better policy than mailing people a check just because they're here," Knott said.

But the idea did find support from others, like House Freedom Caucus Chairman Andy Harris, R-Md.

"I think that hardworking Americans, probably taxpayers, deserve a tax rebate, we’re going to have to discuss how large a rebate that’ll be," Harris told Fox News Digital, suggesting the $5,000 figure should be up for negotiation. "That’s a good idea."

He added that it should go through Congress, potentially through the same mechanism that Republicans used to pass the "One Big, Beautiful Bill Act."

"It would probably have to go through reconciliation," he said.

Republican Study Committee Chairman August Pfluger, R-Texas, suggested the money could come from what the federal government recovers in efforts to crack down on waste, fraud, and abuse of taxpayer dollars.

"Why don't we continue the president's approach towards fraud, and give a dividend to the people of this great country who that money was stolen from?" Pfluger posed, arguing that hundreds of billions of dollars were lost to fraud in the last administration.

Republican Study Committee Chairman Congressman August Pfluger speaks during a press conference with other members of the Republican Study Committee in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 28, 2025. (Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Giving $5,000 to every American adult could cost at least $1 trillion by some estimates, a significant portion of the U.S. annual budget. A price tag that big historically, would be subject to congressional approval, but the president may disagree.

"I think they will do it if we needed it, but I think not," Trump told CBS News when asked if Congress would need to approve the stimulus.

But Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., told CNN's "State of the Union" earlier this week, "I would assume, yes, he'd need Congress to act."

Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

Follow on Twitter at @liz_elkind and send tips to elizabeth.elkind@fox.com

articles.title: Accused Oregon killer indicted in connection with death of sixth woman
articles.excerpt:
Grand jury indicts Jesse Calhoun, 41, on charge of first-degree manslaughter in the death of Elizabeth Gibson

An Oregon man accused of killing five women has been indicted in connection with the deat...
articles.body_text:
Grand jury indicts Jesse Calhoun, 41, on charge of first-degree manslaughter in the death of Elizabeth Gibson

An Oregon man accused of killing five women has been indicted in connection with the death of a sixth woman, officials announced this week.

Jesse Calhoun was indicted by a grand jury on a charge of first-degree manslaughter in the death of Elizabeth “Libby” Gibson, said the Multnomah county district attorney on Wednesday. Calhoun is accused of causing Gibson’s death and acting “unlawfully and recklessly under circumstances manifesting extreme indifference to the value of human life”.

Gibson, who lived in Portland, was 32 when she was last seen in 2022 and reported missing the following year. Officials believe she was killed on or around 18 November 2022 but have not found her body.

Calhoun, 41, has already been charged in the killings of Ashley Real, 22; Kristin Smith, 22; Charity Perry, 24; Bridget Webster, 31; and Joanna Speaks, 32, between 2022 and 2023. He has pleaded not guilty to five counts of second-degree murder and four counts of abuse of a corpse.

“We will not stop. We will do everything in our power to hold him accountable and see that justice is done for each and every one of these victims. We remain committed to these families for as long as it takes,” Nathan Vasquez, the Multnomah county district attorney, said in a statement.

Prosecutors said earlier this year that they plan to try Calhoun for all murders in one trial rather than holding separate proceedings.

Calhoun was previously incarcerated for assaulting a police officer, trying to strangle a police dog, burglary and other charges. He was released early in 2021 for helping fight wildfires through a prison program, but Oregon’s governor’s reversed the decision in 2023 when he came under investigation for the deaths.

Gibson’s family said in a statement that they were “grateful that a definitive step toward justice is finally being taken”.

“Libby was kind, creative, and silly. She welcomed everyone with love and acceptance. Her future was tragically taken from her way too soon,” her siblings said in the statement.

“We are deeply appreciative of the tireless work and dedication of the law enforcement officers and the District Attorney’s Office whose efforts have helped bring us to this point.”

Melissa Marrero, the senior deputy district attorney, said the scope of the investigation had been “enormous”.

“But all information is useful. And to the extent that individuals have been willing to come forward in the past and provide information to us, no matter how small, that information has led us to where we are here today,” she said in a statement.

articles.title: America’s hunters get an exclusive seat at Trump’s White House table as he takes aim at Biden-era rules
articles.excerpt: Former President Donald Trump delivers a patriotic message, urging Americans to reignite the nation's 'indomitable spirit.' Speaking at the Teddy Roosevelt Library dedication, Trump declares America i...
articles.body_text:
Former President Donald Trump delivers a patriotic message, urging Americans to reignite the nation's 'indomitable spirit.' Speaking at the Teddy Roosevelt Library dedication, Trump declares America is now the 'hottest country anywhere in the world,' respected globally. He praises Theodore Roosevelt's profound passion and pride in America, inspiring a renewed sense of national confidence.

FIRST ON FOX: President Donald Trump will host more than 100 hunters, anglers and outdoor industry leaders for dinner at the White House on Thursday night, where he is expected to sign executive orders aimed at expanding hunting and fishing opportunities and reversing certain Biden-era restrictions on hunting and fishing.

Trump will deliver remarks to the sportsmen and industry representatives gathered for the dinner in the Rose Garden as his administration moves to open more public lands and waterways, ease regulatory barriers and promote hunting among younger Americans and veterans, Fox News Digital learned.

He is expected to sign a pair of executive orders in the Oval Office Thursday aimed at expanding "America’s public lands and waterways," promoting healthy wild game populations and expanding access to offshore recreational fishing, a White House official told Fox News Digital.

TRUMP WILL WELCOME FARMERS AND RANCHERS TO WHITE HOUSE DINNER TO CELEBRATE TRADE, TAX WINS

President Donald Trump signs an executive order after delivering remarks on reciprocal tariffs during an event in the Rose Garden entitled "Make America Wealthy Again" at the White House in Washington, DC, on April 2, 2025 (SAUL LOEB/AFP via Getty Images)

Representatives from organizations and companies including Bass Pro Shops, the Cabela Family Foundation, the National Rifle Association, Rocky Mountain Elk Foundation, Yamaha Marine Group, Polaris, Beretta USA, Safari Club International, Primos Hunting, Dallas Safari Club, Outdoor Sportsman Group, Sportsmen’s Alliance, USA Shooting Foundation, Ducks Unlimited, Sportsman Boats, Contender Boats, Taurus Holdings and the Congressional Sportsmen’s Foundation are expected to attend.

America’s outdoor recreation sector generates over $1.2 trillion annually and supports over 5 million jobs, according to a White House official.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, representatives from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and officials from the Commerce Department and NOAA will be present, Fox News Digital learned.

CONGRESS SHOULD HONOR TEDDY ROOSEVELT AND CONSERVE OUR OUTDOORS FOR THE NEXT 250 YEARS

Trump will sign an EO Thursday to open more hunting opportunities on public lands, ease access and regulatory barriers, and promote hunting among younger Americans and veterans. (iStock)

The Secretary of the Interior, the Secretary of Agriculture, the Secretary of War, and the Secretary of Commerce are directed to propose changes to current policies.

One of the policies spotlighted in the order targets Biden-era restrictions on the use of traditional lead ammunition and tackle.

Under Biden, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service adopted station-specific requirements for lead-free ammunition and/or tackle at several national wildlife refuges.

DENNY HAMLIN SAYS FORWARD-FACING SONAR IN PROFESSIONAL BASS FISHING HAS GONE 'A LITTLE OVERBOARD'

Montana officials warned hunters not to attempt to haze or frighten away a bear that has claimed an animal. (iStock)

Trump’s fishing order seeks to unleash more of America’s coastal waters for recreational fishing while cutting federal red tape and giving anglers a bigger role in how fisheries are managed.

The administration seeks to move charter operators toward multi-year permits, replace mail-in catch surveys with mobile reporting, launching programs for depleted stocks such as Atlantic striped bass, and using eligible offshore oil and gas platforms to create artificial reefs.

Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Serbia opens factory to assemble Israeli-made drones
articles.excerpt:
Serbia has opened a factory ⁠to assemble advanced Israeli-made drones, which will supply ⁠the Serbian military and armed forces in other countries.

Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic inaugurated the ...
articles.body_text:
Serbia has opened a factory ⁠to assemble advanced Israeli-made drones, which will supply ⁠the Serbian military and armed forces in other countries.

Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic inaugurated the facility jointly operated with an unnamed Israeli company on Thursday.

“Our plans are huge,” Vucic said in a social media post showing a video of him touring the facility with Israeli Ambassador Avivit Bar-Ilan, adding that at least three more factories will be opened across Serbia with Israeli partners.

Vucic said the facility “will employ around 100 workers and produce state-of-the-art equipment both for the Serbian Armed Forces and the armies of some other countries”.

Vucic did not disclose the factory’s location or the Israeli firm involved, saying journalists were excluded from the opening because of “the confidentiality of the production process”.

Previous reporting by investigative outlet BIRN and Israeli newspaper Haaretz has identified Israeli defence firm Elbit Systems as Serbia’s partner in the drone-manufacturing process.

Elbit has previously been criticised over its role in operations in Gaza and the West Bank.

Last month, Vucic told Serbian news outlet Nezavisne Dnevne Novine that the goal of the factory was to “preserve peace and stability, and to be strong enough to deter all potential aggressors”.

Serbia is one of the few countries in the Western Balkans that is not a NATO member, and it has invested heavily in its military to “preserve neutrality”.

It has faced scrutiny over arms exports to Israel, which BIRN and Haaretz said rose from 1.4 million euros ($1.6 million) in 2023 to 42.3 million euros ($48.5 million) in 2024.

During a visit to Serbia earlier this year, United Nations Special Rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territories Francesca Albanese said Belgrade remained one of Israel’s “most steadfast and determined allies” despite calls for more countries to restrict weapons exports due to the war in Gaza.

articles.title: Outcry as Michigan high school asks girls to share details of menstrual cycles
articles.excerpt:
Students required to disclose information if they wish to make up swimming days lost because of their periods

A Michigan high school is facing scrutiny after parents raised concerns over a gym class ...
articles.body_text:
Students required to disclose information if they wish to make up swimming days lost because of their periods

A Michigan high school is facing scrutiny after parents raised concerns over a gym class policy requiring female students to disclose information about their menstrual cycles if they want to make up swimming days missed because of their periods.

Under the policy, which appears in a Lakeview high school gym syllabus, female students who miss swimming because of their periods must have a parent submit a written note or email identifying the length of their menstrual cycle before they can make up the missed days.

The syllabus states: “Female students will be given the opportunity to make up days, which are missed only because of their menstrual cycle. A written/email note from a parent stating the length of the menstrual duration is required, so the student can make up the days.”

“Students will complete dry land workouts to be able to make up the days,” it continues. “Students will not just sit out. Each day that is not made up will be considered a non-participation day and place the student on the grade reduction scale.”

The requirement caught the attention of Andy Amsdill, whose daughter attends Lakeview high school. Amsdill told WXYZ Detroit that he was stunned when he saw the requirements in her gym syllabus.

“The teacher wants us to either send a note or an email with the suspected length of the cycle which, by itself, is ridiculous,” Amsdill told the outlet.

Menstrual cycle length can sometimes be difficult to predict, and the US National Institutes of Health estimates between 14% to 25% of women experience menstrual irregularities. Irregular periods are even more common in young girls.

Amsdill later told CBS News that other parents contacted him after he spoke publicly about the syllabus, saying they were glad he had brought attention to the issue.

Among them was Bryan Shishakly, whose daughter is now a sophomore at Lakeview. Shishakly said she faced the same requirement during her freshman gym class last year and that it affected her grade.

“My response was like, ‘If they ask, you have no obligation to tell them,’ and it did affect her grade,” Shishakly told CBS. “She’s a straight-A student, and she ended up with a C in gym, and I don’t know how fair that is since it’s only going to apply to the girls at the school.”

Lakeview public schools superintendent Karl D Paulson issued a statement that read: “We recently became aware of a parent’s concern relative to certain class expectations. Given our commitment to partnering with parents to address any issue that might arise, we immediately sought to schedule a meeting with the parent to engage in a conversation about the concern.”

It added: “We look forward to meeting with the parent in the coming days and working collaboratively with that objective. The Lakeview school district remains fully committed to educational excellence and best practices in all it does.”

It remains unclear whether the same requirement appears in other gym class syllabuses at Lakeview high school, or whether the district intends to remove it following the criticism.

The controversy has also prompted Amsdill to question whether the policy could be in violation of title IX, which prohibits sex-based discrimination in education programs or activities that receive federal financial assistance.

Lakeview public schools addresses title IX on its website and includes a separate guide aimed at helping students identify sexual harassment. The guide defines it as “unwanted sexual remarks or behaviors” and says that can include “comments about students’ bodies or how they look or act.”

articles.title: Philadelphia home search uncovers possible human ashes, images of 7 missing women: police
articles.excerpt: Police in Philadelphia give an update on a case after a search of Eugene Horsch's home led to the discovery of over one million images, some containing depictions of missing women appearing unconsciou...
articles.body_text:
Police in Philadelphia give an update on a case after a search of Eugene Horsch's home led to the discovery of over one million images, some containing depictions of missing women appearing unconscious. Credit: FOX 29 Philadelphia

Philadelphia police found images of seven missing women, including two who appear unconscious and injured, while searching more than 1 million images recovered from a home where investigators also found five urns believed to contain human ashes, authorities said Wednesday.

Initial analysis of the images showed two missing women – 27-year-old Gabrielle Armando and 26-year-old Marabel Fresses – lying unconscious in the Chew Avenue home with apparent injuries, Philadelphia Police Department Deputy Commissioner Frank Vanore said in the press conference.

Metadata from the images show they were taken in 2017. "Both women remain missing and have not been seen," Vanore said, adding "to date, neither their bodies nor any DNA evidence have been recovered."

The home belonged to deceased pornographer Raymond "R.C." Horsch and was occupied by his son, Eugene Horsch, whose June arrest sparked the investigation.

CALIFORNIA AUTHORITIES IDENTIFY FINAL UNKNOWN VICTIM OF ‘HAPPY FACE KILLER’ KEITH JESPERSON AFTER 34 YEARS

R.C. Horsch seen in a 1999 mugshot. (S. E. Stokowski/Wikimedia Creative Commons)

On June 19, a Federal Park Ranger arrested Eugene Horsch, 44, after investigating him and a female passenger sitting in a BMW outside of Philadelphia's Independence Mall, Vanore explained.

"During the course of that investigation, officers recovered two firearms, narcotics, and identification impersonating a federal law enforcement officer, and he was charged. Task force officers from the DEA were able to develop probable cause that same day and serve a warrant on Mr. Horsch's residence," Vanore said.

The female passenger presented police with a false identification using the name Blair Tonzelli, a woman who has been missing since 2023, a spokesperson for the Philadelphia Police Department confirmed to Fox News Digital.

FOUL ODOR AT NYC SCHOOL LEADS POLICE TO BODY HIDDEN IN CHIMNEY

A photo of Blair Tonzelli, who went missing in February 2023. (National Missing and Unidentified Persons System (NAMUS))

The true identity of the woman in the vehicle has not been released. Tonzelli's whereabouts remain unknown.

After obtaining a warrant, investigators found "a homemade laboratory of some kind in the basement area, five urns believed to contain human ashes, and a large amount of digital evidence — including computers, hard drives, flash drives, DVRs, cameras, and phones," Vanore said during the press conference.

Investigators have identified 58 total people in the videos and images they found in the home. Vanore said "four of those identified appear lifeless, with video depicting what may have happened to one of them."

NEW CALIFORNIA LAW EXPANDS DNA TOOLS FOR MISSING PERSONS INVESTIGATIONS

Eugene Horsch's mugshot. (FOX 29 Philadelphia)

One video shows R.C. Horsch handcuffing a woman to a bed and zip-tying her neck until she became unconscious. Police identified this woman as Nicole Fusaro, according to FOX 29 Philadelphia.

Another missing woman connected to the home is R.C. Horsch's ex-wife, Amy McHale, who has been missing since 2016, FOX 29 reported.

Two other missing women have been connected to the home. Police identified one as a 25-year-old woman but did not name her, and the other has yet to be identified, according to FOX 29.

Image of Marabel Fresses, who went missing in 2018. (National Missing and Unidentified Persons System (NAMUS))

"We have only processed a small fraction of the total media. Thousands of videos remain to be analyzed. We are working to corroborate what we see and gather physical evidence to prove our findings, supported throughout by the FBI as we determine our next steps," Vanore concluded Wednesday.

articles.title: Charles sounded 'giddily elated' after Diana’s death, claims Earl Spencer
articles.excerpt:
In latest extracts from upcoming memoir, Diana’s brother suggests some in Buckingham Palace were ‘relieved’ at her death

The brother of the late Diana, Princess of Wales, has claimed in published ext...
articles.body_text:
In latest extracts from upcoming memoir, Diana’s brother suggests some in Buckingham Palace were ‘relieved’ at her death

The brother of the late Diana, Princess of Wales, has claimed in published extracts of his new memoir that King Charles sounded “giddily elated – like a lottery winner” in a phone call to him immediately after her death.

Earl Spencer also says he believed Buckingham Palace wanted William and Harry and himself to walk behind Diana’s coffin because the then Prince Charles was “adamant” he was going to walk and palace officials feared “members of the public might shout abuse at him”.

By getting Diana’s sons to walk, “that would surely guarantee against insults flying”, he wrote.

The memoir, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, due to be published next week, has already made headlines, with Spencer alleging that during a heated phone call before Diana’s funeral, the king remarked: “Rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough.”

Buckingham Palace issued a robust rebuttal on Wednesday evening, saying in a statement: “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss.”

In new extracts, published on Thursday on the website of the Daily Mail, which is serialising the book, Spencer suggests that some inside Buckingham Palace were “relieved – indeed pleased” at Diana’s death in a Paris car crash. It was his suspicion that Charles’s first reaction must have been to think how he could now marry Camilla Parker Bowles.

According to Spencer, Diana had confided in a friend that days before their wedding, Charles had told her “she needed to know he was very happy to marry her, but he was not actually in love with her”, and she was certain he was “entering their marriage with his heart elsewhere”.

Diana tried to break off the engagement after finding a bracelet Charles had bought for Camilla, who is now the queen, he writes. But their father was “appalled”, telling her “it was impossible to pull out of such an enormous commitment at that point”.

Spencer says in the book that he also believes Charles may have contributed to the princess’s eating disorder, saying Diana’s waist shrank from 29in to 23.5in between the engagement and wedding after she was “devastated” at her fiance squeezing her waist and saying: ‘Oh, a bit chubby here, aren’t we.”

He was also convinced Diana had ADHD and, like himself, suffered from Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria. He writes: “It is a sad fact that, in her later years, Diana drove herself more than once to Beachy Head, the highest chalk sea cliff in England, while contemplating ending it all. Her love for her sons stopped her from going further.”

The excerpt goes on to say that Diana told him she was going to get divorced and that “my husband is in love with his valet”.

Spencer, 62, has said he wrote the memoir to correct “untruths” told about his elder sister.

The row over the book overshadowed a busy day for the royal family, with the Duke of Sussex also entered the mix with an engagement of his own.

Harry, who it is understood was aware of his uncle’s book in advance but not its contents, arrived at the inaugural Invictus Spirit awards in London on Thursday evening in his first appearance since returning to the UK from the US last month.

The Prince and Princess of Wales were on their first official trip to the Isle of Bute off the west coast of Scotland. The couple, who hold the titles of Duke and Duchess of Rothesay in Scotland, visited the namesake town of Rothesay, dropped in at a shinty club and stopped at a pub while meeting community leaders and volunteers.

Charles, meanwhile, was appearing in public for the first time since Spencer’s allegations were aired, at an AI summit he had convened at Dumfries House, in Ayrshire. Addressing global tech leaders, he warned of the “existential dangers” of AI systems falling into the wrong hands.

As those who have created these technologies had warned, AI risked “developing darker capacities – perhaps even to take life”, he said. The king spoke of the need for reassurance that “our humanity remains sacred” and “that we will not lose control of our destiny, or our souls”.

articles.title: Far-left streamer Hasan Piker called out by MS NOW hosts in fiery exchange over him being a drag for Democrats
articles.excerpt: MS NOW host Symone Sanders Townsend told Hasan Piker during an interview on her "Clock It" podcast that she would tell candidates to absolutely "disavow" the far-left streamer because she wants to win...
articles.body_text:
MS NOW host Symone Sanders Townsend told Hasan Piker during an interview on her "Clock It" podcast that she would tell candidates to absolutely "disavow" the far-left streamer because she wants to win.

Far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker clashed with two MS NOW hosts on Wednesday on multiple issues, including his political influence and his anti-Israel stance, as Symone Sanders Townsend told the streamer point-blank she would be telling candidates she worked for to absolutely "disavow" him.

"I used to work campaigns, Hasan, and I have to tell you, if I was a strategist or a consultant or the political director on one of these campaigns, I would absolutely be telling my people to disavow you," Sanders Townsend told Piker in an interview on her "Clock It" podcast, which she co-hosts with Eugene Daniels. "I really would, because we wanna win! We wanna win, and so, like, if you’re not gonna help people win, distance."

Piker acknowledged the disagreement between them as Townsend continued, "I’ve elected people, though. You’ve never elected anybody."

STEPHEN A SMITH WARNS HASAN PIKER WILL ‘CONTAMINATE’ DEMOCRATS IN THE MIDTERMS, ‘COME BACK TO HAUNT THEM’

Twitch streamer Hasan Piker claimed that AIPAC was behind the wave of Democrats criticizing his rhetoric. (Florencia Tan Jun/Web Summit via Sportsfile via Getty Images)

Piker also maintained his view that Israel is worse than Hamas, though he acknowledged it was a provocative statement. "I do believe that," he said.

"Is Hamas a religious fundamentalist operation that have engaged in violent actions? Of course they have, absolutely," Piker continued. "But that violence is directly born out of, and even that repression is directly born out of, the conditions brought about by the occupation that's been going on for 80 plus years."

Daniels pressed the Twitch streamer on whether he understood that it sounded like he was endorsing violence by making that argument.

"Do you understand that that's how people hear it? And is that what you are endorsing?" Daniels asked.

"So this, again, goes back to the same — this goes back to the same dynamic, right?" Piker said. "Structural violence and state violence is oftentimes made to be invisible. So when Israel as a state is operating its normal state functions, and sometimes it can come across as excessive, right? It's not seen as violent."

"It's no different than when people protest against police violence and police brutality. The brutality of the police is systemic violence, and therefore it's normalized," he added.

"It's made to be invisible," Piker continued. "Whereas when people protest against the police, that is all of a sudden chaotic, that's all of a sudden violent. It's never violent when the police actually release tear gas on protesters. It's violence if the protesters use leaf blowers to blow that tear gas."

Townsend jumped in to reject the comparison to protesting the police.

"I'm gonna let Eugene move on, but I just want to note, it sounds like the example that you just gave that the people who are protesting the police are Hamas. And I just would reject that as somebody who has protested the police before, but we can move on," Townsend said.

HASAN PIKER IS BECOMING THE 'FACE OF THE PROGRESSIVE MOVEMENT,' FORMER DEMOCRATIC OPERATIVE WARNS

MS NOW hosts Symone Sanders Townsend and Eugene Daniels interviewed far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker in an episode of their "Clock It" podcast on September 17, 2026. (Paul Morigi/Getty Images; Florencia Tan Jun/Web Summit via Sportsfile via Getty Images; William B. Plowman/NBC via Getty Images)

"Symone Sanders Townsend is putting her finger on a real tension for Democrats heading into the midterms," David Scharf, chair of Morrison Cohen’s Government Strategies & Controversies practice, told Fox News Digital. "Hasan Piker gives candidates access to a large, young audience that traditional political media often doesn't reach. But he also gives Republicans a ready-made way to force those candidates to answer for statements they didn't make."

"Every candidate on the record defending him, appearing with him, or refusing to distance themselves from him helps turn him into a campaign issue," he added.

"In safe blue districts, that may not matter," Scharf said. "In a race as close as Michigan's Senate contest, it can. That's why Sanders Townsend, who has actually run campaigns, is looking at this very differently than Piker is. He's building an audience. She's counting votes."

RASKIN CALLS PIKER’S RHETORIC 'IRRELEVANT DISTRACTION' AFTER THE STREAMER SAID HE'D VOTE FOR HAMAS OVER ISRAEL

Hasan Piker has backed several candidates in primaries across the country ahead of the midterm elections, including Francesca Hong, who lost Wisconsin's Democratic gubernatorial primary in August 2026. (Joshua Lott/Getty Images)

Piker insisted during a Friday livestream it was his "God-given" and "constitutionally protected right" to proclaim hatred for America.

During one of his lengthy shows, Piker responded to an attack ad against Democratic Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed based on his connection to Piker and his past controversial statements claiming to "hate" America.

"Bro, I hate this country, dude. I hate America," Piker said in clips featured on the ad. "Oh God, I f---ing hate America so much."

Piker argued after showing the clip that it was "clear" that he was angry at "what America as the American government is doing to Americans and to everyone else" but nevertheless defended his right to say he hates the country.

EL-SAYED GRILLED ON PIKER, ISRAEL AND SOCIALIST TIES AFTER MIKE ROGERS SKIPS SENATE DEBATE

Twitch streamer Hasan Piker appeared on the campaign trail with Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo)

"Of course, I'm a Godd--- American. It is my Godd--- God-given and constitutionally protected right to say I hate America if America is actually f---ing over Americans," he said. "You can clip chimp it all day. It doesn't change that. It doesn't change that mentality."

"To present this as like, oh, 'These guys are real America haters' as some liberals have been doing on the timeline, as virtually the entirety of the Republican Party is doing, is so f---ing stupid," Piker added.

Hanna Panreck is an associate editor at Fox News.

articles.title: Husband and wife get trapped in premier hiking destination; only one of them makes it out alive
articles.excerpt:
The 70-year-old Michigan man, Craig Berg, was found injured and suffering from hypothermia after disappearing during an extended solo hike. (U.S. Coast Guard Great Lakes)

A sudden and powerful storm ...
articles.body_text:
The 70-year-old Michigan man, Craig Berg, was found injured and suffering from hypothermia after disappearing during an extended solo hike. (U.S. Coast Guard Great Lakes)

A sudden and powerful storm over Washington state's Cascade Mountains quickly turned a challenging hike into a fight for survival by an Oklahoma couple.

The pair was navigating the rugged "core zone" of the remote Enchantments wilderness when they were engulfed by heavy, deep snow.

By late afternoon, the freezing, high-elevation conditions brought their trek to a desperate halt.

2 MYSTERY DEATHS AT ZION NATIONAL PARK PROMPT URGENT QUESTIONS ABOUT VISITOR SAFETY

At 5:26 p.m., the husband sent an urgent text to 911.

He reported to dispatchers that their clothes were soaked through from the storm and his wife was physically unable to continue moving, according to FOX 13 Seattle.

A woman died after she and her husband became stranded in deep snow while hiking Washington state's remote Enchantments. (Greg Vaughn/VW Pics/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

The stranded hiker, identified as 45-year-old Sybil Claborn of Oklahoma City, succumbed to the extreme elements and died in the snow on Sunday.

Before the rescue team reached them, Claborn's husband tried to carry her out but was unable to do so.

They were stranded at an elevation of roughly 7,000 to 8,000 feet, about 8 to 10 miles from the nearest trailheads.

TEEN HIKER'S DISAPPEARANCE ENDS IN TRAGEDY AT NATIONAL PARK WITH KEY QUESTION REMAINING

The situation prompted a frantic rescue effort involving multiple agencies — but the severe weather repeatedly thwarted attempts to reach the couple by air.

The sheriff's office requested a hoist-equipped helicopter at 6:51 p.m., and an Army helicopter launched from Yakima shortly after 8 p.m.

A husband and wife were hiking the Enchantments when severe weather left the couple (not pictured) stranded miles from nearby trailheads. (Greg Vaughn/VW Pics/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

Stormy conditions forced the helicopter to turn back as the husband remained in contact with 911 and reported that Claborn's condition was deteriorating.

A second Army helicopter attempt around 10:50 p.m. was also unsuccessful — while Chelan County Mountain Rescue crews continued toward the couple on foot.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Ground crews finally reached the stranded hikers around 3:30 a.m., finding Claborn dead and her husband suffering from severe hypothermia.

Her husband was warmed inside a tent before he was transported to Cascade Medical Center in Leavenworth for treatment.

The Enchantments, pictured above. were experiencing stormy conditions when a husband and wife became stranded in deep snow while hiking. (Greg Vaughn/VW Pics/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

Claborn's body was later recovered and taken to the Chelan County Coroner's Office.

Authorities are actively investigating the cause and manner of Claborn's death.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Chelan County Sheriff's Office for more information.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

While the tragedy in the Enchantments unfolded amid heavy snow and freezing conditions, other hikers have died this year while battling extreme heat.

The Enchantments are known for their dramatic alpine scenery, high-elevation lakes and rugged, challenging terrain. (Greg Vaughn/VW Pics/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

Earlier this summer, a 68-year-old French tourist died after attempting to hike to safety after his vehicle became stuck in mud in Death Valley National Park.

A similar tragedy unfolded at the Grand Canyon in June.

That month, an 18-year-old hiker died after developing heat-related symptoms on the park’s Bright Angel Trail, the National Park Service said.

Andrea Margolis is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital and Fox Business. Readers can follow her on X at @andreamargs or send story tips to andrea.margolis@fox.com.

articles.title: US secures release of detained citizen Adam Castillo in Myanmar
articles.excerpt:
The United States State Department has helped to secure the release of Adam Castillo, a US citizen detained in Myanmar for three months.

A delegation of US officials travelled to ⁠Myanmar’s capital, ...
articles.body_text:
The United States State Department has helped to secure the release of Adam Castillo, a US citizen detained in Myanmar for three months.

A delegation of US officials travelled to ⁠Myanmar’s capital, Naypyidaw, last week to speak with local officials about his case, the State Department said on Thursday.

Myanmar state media reported that Castillo, 40, was flown out of the capital “in consideration of the friendly relations between Myanmar and the United States”. State media said he had been charged with breach of trust allegations, and that he had violated the regulations of the American Chamber of Commerce in Myanmar, a business group for which he served as president.

Castillo was released into the custody of US officials and then flew to Bangkok, Thailand.

“We are thrilled to see Adam coming home and are grateful for the collaboration and efforts from the Trump administration,” said Mickey Bergman, CEO of Global Reach, a Washington-based nonprofit that helped Castillo’s family advocate for his release, referring to US President Donald Trump.

“I can’t wait to welcome my brother home, but I know it will be bittersweet for him,” said his sister Amanda Castillo in a statement. “He had such great hopes for enhanced US/Myanmar relations, and he holds the deepest respect for the Burmese people, among whom he lived for many years.”

The former US Marine, who was a founder and owner of the security risk management firm AGS Myanmar, was detained at Yangon International Airport on June 11 after returning from Malaysia.

The arrest came after the American Chamber of Commerce in Myanmar accused him of financial impropriety, which he denies. At the time, Myanmar authorities would only say he had been arrested because “there was a crime and a lawsuit”, but did not provide further details.

articles.title: Fresh activity emerges at Iran’s deeply buried nuclear site as Trump warns Iran not to ‘get cute’
articles.excerpt:
FDD’s Behnam Ben Taleblu says Iran’s deeply buried nuclear-linked site poses a growing military challenge as Tehran hardens entrances and rebuilds sensitive facilities.

New satellite imagery shows Ir...
articles.body_text:
FDD’s Behnam Ben Taleblu says Iran’s deeply buried nuclear-linked site poses a growing military challenge as Tehran hardens entrances and rebuilds sensitive facilities.

New satellite imagery shows Iran has added new defenses around tunnel entrances at Pickaxe Mountain, the deeply buried nuclear-linked site President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened to strike, as Russia and China on Thursday vetoed a U.S.-drafted Security Council resolution aimed at preserving international monitoring of sanctions on Tehran.

The Institute for Science and International Security said in a report released Thursday that satellite imagery from Sept. 11 shows earthen roadblocks remain in place on roads leading to Pickaxe Mountain’s western tunnel portals near the Natanz nuclear complex. The institute said the continued restricted access reinforces its assessment that the facility is not currently being used for normal operations, while assessing that valuable equipment or materials remain inside.

The report also identified additional soil placed over one western tunnel portal and over a nearby cluster of entrances first built in 2007. The institute said the added soil increases the amount of earth protecting the entrances and helps harden them against aerial bombardment.

EXPERTS ‘DEEPLY’ CONCERNED OVER IRAN’S WORK AT UNDERGROUND NUCLEAR SITE

An overview of Iran’s Natanz nuclear complex and nearby Pickaxe Mountain, seen in satellite imagery from Aug. 21, 2026. (Satellite image ©2026 Vantor Technologies.)

The findings come one week after Trump issued his latest warning over Pickaxe Mountain.

"We notice there’s a little activity at Pickaxe," Trump told reporters last week. "I would advise Iran not to get cute because we will have to hit them very hard."

Trump has repeatedly raised the possibility of attacking the site. In a July 28 "Fox & Friends" interview highlighted by the White House, Trump said the U.S. was watching Pickaxe closely and knew "exactly what’s going on," adding that Washington could "take out Pickaxe" if diplomacy failed.

Pickaxe Mountain lies roughly two kilometers from Natanz and features multiple tunnel entrances leading into a deeply buried underground complex. Construction began in 2020 following sabotage that damaged an advanced centrifuge assembly facility at Natanz, and Iranian officials subsequently said a replacement underground facility was being built for advanced centrifuge production. Analysts estimate portions of the facility may be buried at least 100 meters beneath the mountain. Iran has said there is no nuclear activity at the site.

TRUMP SAYS US HAS 'MASSIVE' MUNITIONS STOCKPILE, VOWS 'TREASONOUS' LEAKERS BEING HUNTED DOWN

A closer view of tunnel entrances at Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, near the Natanz nuclear complex, seen in satellite imagery from Aug. 21, 2026. (Satellite image ©2026 Vantor Technologies)

Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital that some analysts believe the opportunity for a straightforward strike on Pickaxe Mountain may already have passed.

"The window to strike Pickaxe Mountain, according to some, has already expired because the regime has dug an underground nuclear facility several times deeper than Fordow," Ben Taleblu said. But he argued that Washington retains military options even if destroying the underground complex itself proves difficult.

"Washington can do what it’s traditionally been able to do with sites that are underground, hardened and fortified, and that’s to bury their entrances and raise the political cost to the Islamic Republic of being able to dig out," he said.

"While there may not be the perfect munition just yet, Uncle Sam always has a bigger bomb," Ben Taleblu added. "And in the meantime, what they can do is show that they mean business by burying the entrances."

NUCLEAR EXPERTS URGE TRUMP NOT TO LET IRAN STEER TALKS AWAY FROM REGIME'S ATOMIC THREAT

A satellite view shows an overview of the Natanz nuclear facility and Pickaxe Mountain, near Natanz, Iran, June 30, 2026 (Vantor/Handout via Reuters)

The Pickaxe findings came alongside signs of reconstruction at another sensitive Iranian facility.

In a separate report Thursday, the institute said Iran was "rapidly moving forward" with reconstruction of Taleghan 2 at the Parchin military complex southeast of Tehran. Vantor Technologies satellite imagery from Sept. 13 shows Iran erected a tarp over the destroyed hardened facility, obscuring work underneath from satellite or aerial observation, while dump trucks, bulldozers, concrete equipment and cranes were active around the site.

The institute said Iran also built new concrete reinforcement that could provide additional protection against aerial attack. Taleghan 2 was struck by Israel in October 2024 and again in March 2026 after Iran had rebuilt and hardened the facility. The institute said significant questions remain about Tehran’s plans for the site.

The military developments unfolded alongside a separate confrontation over Iran at the United Nations.

CHINA ORDERS FIRMS TO IGNORE US IRAN SANCTIONS, DARING US TO ENFORCE CRACKDOWN

Satellite imagery shows the underlying structure of the rebuilt Taleghan 2 facility at Iran’s Parchin military complex encased within a concrete "sarcophagus," prior to being covered with soil in February 13, 2026. (Vantor Technologies with annotations by ISIS)

Russia and China on Thursday vetoed a US-authored Security Council resolution that would have extended for another year, until September 2027, the mandate of the Panel of Experts supporting the 1737 Iran Sanctions Committee. The measure received 11 votes in favor, while Pakistan and Somalia abstained.

The panel investigates alleged sanctions violations and reports on implementation. The dispute reflects a deeper split over whether UN sanctions suspended under the 2015 nuclear agreement were legally restored through the "snapback" mechanism. Most Council members maintain that the sanctions and related monitoring structures were revived, while Russia and China reject the legal and procedural validity of that position.

A day before the vote, U.S. Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz told reporters in New York that Washington considers the sanctions legally restored.

"The snapback sanctions … occurred, the United States and this UN Security Council followed appropriate procedures for that to occur," Waltz said Wednesday at a news conference attended by Fox News Digital. "Those sanctions are in place and we expect those who are a party to fully enforce those sanctions."

Waltz said the expert panel is important because sanctioned companies and individuals can attempt to evade restrictions by changing names and corporate structures.

"The president has been clear and the world community has been clear with resolution after resolution that the Iranian regime cannot have a nuclear weapon," Waltz said.

Imagery shows Iranian military facility being buried and fortified. (Images via Vantor with annotations from ISIS)

Thursday also brought fresh UN scrutiny of both Washington and Tehran. An independent UN fact-finding mission said it had reasonable grounds to believe two U.S. strikes on civilian sites in Iran in February constituted war crimes, while separately concluding that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their crackdown on anti-government protests. The mission is investigative rather than judicial, and its findings do not themselves constitute criminal judgments.

Fox News Digital reached out to Iran U.N. mission for comments but didn’t receive them in time for publication.

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict, global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

articles.title: ‘I’m genuinely sorry’: Australian Hyrox athlete who soiled herself apologises to China and rivals
articles.excerpt:
Joanna Wietrzyk ‘regrets’ decision to keep racing

She forfeits points from her win in the Beijing race

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

The Australian athlete who caused ...
articles.body_text:
Joanna Wietrzyk ‘regrets’ decision to keep racing

She forfeits points from her win in the Beijing race

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

The Australian athlete who caused a storm by winning a Hyrox event in China despite soiling herself during the race has apologised to the “people of China” and rival athletes in a statement online.

Posting on Instagram, Joanna Wietrzyk, said she offered a “sincere apology” to the “people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the Hyrox organizers for what happened during the race in Beijing”.

Footage of Wietrzyk, a world record holder, went viral after it showed her competing in – and winning – Saturday’s event with demanding exercises and using communal equipment, despite having faecal matter running down her legs.

But she admitted in her post on Thursday night that she should have “stepped off the track” and that there is “more to life than racing”.

“I felt completely fit and healthy at the start of the race, with no reason to expect any illness,” Wietrzyk wrote.

“Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognize that I should have made a different choice. I take responsibility for my decision to continue and am deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption it caused.”

Furhtermore, she said, she would forfeit the points from winning the event.
 ”I know my actions had an impact beyond myself, and I am genuinely sorry to everyone who was affected. I am learning from this experience and will carry those lessons with me, including remembering that there is more to life than racing and knowing when it is right to step away. On reflection, I have decided to retroactively withdraw from the race and forfeit the points I earned.”

Hyrox, an increasingly popular fitness competition launched in Germany in 2017, is now held in locations across the world. It debuted in mainland China in late 2024.

In each race, participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing fitness exercises at shared high-intensity stations – including a rowing machine, sled pushes, burpee jumps, medicine ball throws and lunges while carrying a sandbag.

Ending her statement, Wietrzyk said: “Thank you to those standing by me, both as an athlete and as a person, during this time, and to everyone who has reached out with kindness and support. It means more to me than I can properly express right now. I will be taking some time to recover, reflect and look after myself and my family away from the noise.”

articles.title: Trump’s $5K checks could join stack of past unfulfilled promises, former Congress budget chief warns
articles.excerpt: A top economist who worked to set government economic policy is warning the President Donald Trump’s plan to send cash payments to Americans likely won’t pan out, and that the plans have serious impli...
articles.body_text:
A top economist who worked to set government economic policy is warning the President Donald Trump’s plan to send cash payments to Americans likely won’t pan out, and that the plans have serious implications for the American Dream.

President Donald Trump's latest cash promise to Americans is unlikely to come to fruition, just like others before it, an economist and former congressional budget hawk told Fox News Digital.

"So the president has promised a lot of checks, the most recent being $5,000 to every American if Republicans hold on to the House and Senate. We ever going to see these? Well, I don't think so," said Douglas Holz-Eakin, president of fiscal policy think tank American Action Forum.

Holz-Eakin previously served as the director of the Congressional Budget Office, and as the director of domestic and economic policy for late Republican Sen. John McCain's 2008 presidential campaign.

TRUMP DEFENDS $5,000 DIVIDEND PROPOSAL, PRAISES 'BEAUTIFUL' TARIFFS ON 'INGRAHAM ANGLE'

Trump has repeatedly defended tariffs as a key pillar of his economic agenda, saying they will bring manufacturing back to the United States and generate revenue as Republicans seek to hold Congress in the November elections. (Mike Kropf/Getty Images)

"The DOGE checks were never realistic because DOGE was never going to save that much money," said Holz-Eakin in reference to the Elon Musk-led Department of Government Efficiency's sweeping layoffs and budget cuts to federal agencies.

He continued: "And the tariff checks were never that realistic because [Trump] didn't have the authority to issue the checks, and that's actually true of all of these promises."

Holz-Eakin also mentioned the Trump administration's recently-proposed plan to give $9,000 checks to stay-at-home-mothers likely won't come through either.

"Trying to get money to stay at home moms for childcare, there's a route to that, but it's gonna be tough ... we'll see if they actually pull it off," he said. "So, I would be skeptical that any of these checks are gonna be in your mailbox very soon."

The internationally-known economist likened the Trump administration's fiscal policy to that of former President Joe Biden's Democratic administration.

"I think we've seen two successive administrations get themselves in the following position: inflation is too high and wages aren't keeping up with it. Well, that's failing at the American dream," Holz-Eakin explained.

THE FED JUST THREW A WRENCH IN TRUMP'S MIDTERM ECONOMIC MESSAGE

He said that getting inflation under control was the first step in restoring order, as well as being "utterly supportive" of the Federal Reserve, which Holz-Eatin says is working to achieve that goal.

The Fed hiked interest rates Wednesday for the first time in three years, and signaled that more rate increases could be coming. This comes despite Trump's push to have the world's most powerful central bank lower interest rates to lessen the monthly burden on American's seeking home and auto loans.

US national debt hits $40 trillion for the first time and there is little relief in sight. (Fox News)

"Inflation remains elevated," the Federal Open Market Committee said in a post-meeting statement. "Today’s policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee’s 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability."

"You need to have, I think, a more vibrant economy, and this economy is doing okay, but it's putting up with a lot of headwinds," said Holz-Eatin.

He named specific Trump administration policy decisions he says are to blame for the lackluster economy, which has burdened the middle class as grocery prices continue to rise.

"The first headwinds were tariffs, second headwinds were the the oil prices and fight with Iran, and we need to get past those battles and, and let the economy just go, and ... that would be a better environment for the families," he told Fox News Digital.

CONGRESS SPENDS $7 TRILLION. HERE’S HOW THAT MATH WORKS OUT IF YOU THINK OF JUST $100

President Donald Trump presents Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell with what he Trump called a list of cost overruns for the Federal Reserve’s $2.5 billion headquarters renovation project on July 24, 2025 in Washington, DC. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

As for overall fiscal policy, Holz-Eatin says he's worried that the country is going in the wrong direction when it comes to economic and fiscal policy.

"I'm a former director of the Congressional Budget Office. I have to every day get up and look at the books and wonder, 'how's this going to add up?'" he said. "And right now it doesn't add up."

"We're $41 trillion in debt. The deficit is $2 trillion every year and it's getting larger. You can't just keep putting people on the on government programs. It won't add up."

He proposed a fix — reverting to "old school conservative" politics.

"I'd like to see a bit of a U-turn that got the debt under control, didn't spend quite so much money, and got through this without having to raise our taxes. So, that sounds like an old school conservative plan to me, but that's not what we're seeing right now."

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment on Trump's economic promises, but did not hear back at time of publication.

Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Idaho prosecutors accuse Bryan Kohberger of 'fishing' to find better arguments for bid to withdraw guilty plea
articles.excerpt:
Legal maneuvers escalate in the Idaho student murders case as Bryan Kohberger attempts to disqualify Judge Steven Hippler. Fox News legal analyst Gregg Jarrett breaks down the defense's strategy.

Ida...
articles.body_text:
Legal maneuvers escalate in the Idaho student murders case as Bryan Kohberger attempts to disqualify Judge Steven Hippler. Fox News legal analyst Gregg Jarrett breaks down the defense's strategy.

Idaho prosecutors are accusing Bryan Kohberger's new legal team of attempting a "fishing expedition" and trying to buy time to find better arguments for his bid to withdraw his guilty plea.

"Unfortunately for [Kohberger], that is not how discovery in post-conviction proceedings works," Deputy Latah County Prosecuting Attorney Keith Scholl wrote in a response to the convicted killer's request for more time to file an amended petition.

The deadline is currently set for Nov. 13 — four years to the day since the Idaho student murders in Moscow.

BRYAN KOHBERGER’S 2027 HEARING IS NOT GUARANTEED AS IDAHO SEEKS QUICK DISMISSAL

Bryan Kohberger appears at the Ada County Courthouse for his sentencing hearing on July 23, 2025, in Boise, Idaho. Kohberger pleaded guilty in exchange for being spared the death penalty for the stabbing of four University of Idaho students nearly three years ago. (Kyle Green-Pool/Getty Images)

Kohberger's lawyers argue that the deadline would force them to irrevocably waive any claims not included in the amended petition, which is due before discovery deadlines set for next year. They want to see discovery materials before filing it.

"Post-conviction discovery is supposed to assist you and your lawyers in proving a legitimate constitutional claim, in this case, ineffective assistance of counsel," said Randolph Rice, a Maryland-based attorney and legal analyst who has been following the case.

Madison Mogen, top left, smiles on the shoulders of her best friend, Kaylee Goncalves, as they pose with Ethan Chapin, Xana Kernodle, and two other housemates in Goncalves' final Instagram post, shared the day before the four students were stabbed to death. (@kayleegoncalves/Instagram)

"It isn't supposed to be a fishing expedition to help you invent a new one," he added. "You don't get to throw a fishing net into the discovery ocean and hope you pull up a constitutional violation."

ATTORNEY WHO DEFENDED DC SNIPER SAYS KOHBERGER FACES 'MONUMENTAL UPHILL BATTLE' UNDOING GUILTY PLEA

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Prosecutors have also filed a motion to dismiss Kohberger's handwritten petition outright, but that is not expected to succeed given the likelihood that his lawyers will replace it with a new amended petition.

Judge Steven Hippler gave Bryan Kohberger's new legal team until Nov. 13 to amend Kohberger's handwritten filing. (Katherine Jones/Idaho Statesman/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Kohberger pleaded guilty on July 2, 2025, to four counts of first-degree murder and a burglary charge for the stabbing deaths of 21-year-olds Madison Mogen and Kaylee Goncalves as well as 20-year-olds Xana Kernodle and Ethan Chapin.

Latah County Prosecutor, Bill Thompson walks across the carpark at Latah County Courthouse, Moscow, Idaho, Friday, Aug. 7, 2026. (Derek Shook for Fox News Digital)

BRYAN KOHBERGER CLAIMS FAMILY JOINED PLEA TALKS AS HE SEEKS TO WITHDRAW GUILTY PLEA: COURT DOCS

A year later, he claimed in a self-produced motion for post-conviction relief that he had ineffective counsel and was duped into pleading guilty by his former defense attorneys.

BRYAN KOHBERGER GETS NEW ATTORNEY APPOINTED AFTER HE ASKS COURT FOR POST-CONVICTION RELIEF IN IDAHO MURDERS

Judge Steven Hippler gave his new legal team until Nov. 13 to amend Kohberger's handwritten filing.

Bryan Kohberger arrives at Monroe County Courthouse in Pennsylvania in advance of his extradition hearing. (The Image Direct for Fox News Digital)

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

The convicted killer's lawyers have separately filed a motion to disqualify Hippler from overseeing the case, citing concerns of potential bias, and to change the venue back to Latah County, where the crimes took place.

A still image from bodycam video shows Bryan Kohberger in an Aug. 21, 2022 traffic stop in Latah County, Idaho. (Latah County Sheriff's Office)

BRYAN KOHBERGER'S VICTIMS 'ENDURED A HIGH DEGREE OF PAIN' AND SUFFERING, UNSEALED AUTOPSY REPORTS SHOW

Kohberger's criminal defense team had previously changed the venue out of Latah County. The court moved it to Ada County to address fair trial concerns.

The Latah County Prosecuting Attorney's Office and Kohberger's new lead lawyer Greg Rauch are both based in the county seat of Moscow.

Fox News Digital reached out to prosecutors and Kohberger's team.

articles.title: Democratic candidates hold narrow leads in Texas and Michigan US Senate races, new poll shows – live

New polling shows that margins in Texas and Michigan’s key Senate r...
articles.body_text:
James Talarico and Abdul El-Sayed are ahead – but by a razor-thin margin, according to a new poll from Emerson College and The Hill

New polling shows that margins in Texas and Michigan’s key Senate races remain razor-thin, with Democrats just narrowly in the lead.

The new poll from Emerson College and The Hill puts James Talarico, the Democratic challenger in Texas, up by just one percent against Republican nominee Ken Paxton.

The prospect of flipping a Senate seat in deep-red Texas has long seemed a Democrat pipe dream. The last meaningfully competitive Senate race in the state was 6 years ago, when former Texas congressman Beto O’Rourke came within three percentage points of ousting Republican senator Ted Cruz.

But it’s seemed closer to becoming a reality ever since Paxton, the scandal-plagued Texas attorney general, unseated incumbent John Cornyn in a primary race with President Trump’s backing.

In Michigan, the poll found that progressive firebrand Abdul El-Sayed is faring slightly better against Republican Mike Rogers, a former congressman, with El-Sayed winning 48 percent of respondents’ support compared to Rogers’ 46 percent. Rogers, the poll found, wins out with non-college educated voters and older Michiganders, while El-Sayed is ahead with independents.

The Texas poll found that Democrats haven’t won over as many voters in the state’s race for governor, with challenger Gina Hinojosa lagging sitting governor Greg Abbott by 3 percent.

Maria Elvira Salazar, a Republican congresswoman from South Florida, made a rare public break with President Trump in a new ad, pushing back against Trump’s hardline immigration policy.

“Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” Salazar said, speaking directly into the camera.

Salazar’s ad, framed as a personal message to Trump, highlights the large percentage of people recently detained by ICE who had no criminal record – part of Trump’s aggressive mass deportation campaign that voters have increasingly soured on.

“Be careful what your advisors are telling you about immigration policy,” Rep. Salazar told Trump, looking directly into the camera. “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.”

Salazar continued: “You can be for immigration what Lincoln was for slavery and Reagan was for communism. I’m not talking about giving them amnesty. I’m talking about giving them a dignified life in this promised land.”

Salazar’s rebuke comes as Trump is making every effort to make the midterm elections a referendum on his second term in office, a prospect that has worried some Republicans concerned about the president’s waning popularity dragging down their odds.

A group of Democratic senators is demanding information from the Trump administration about what’s being done with massive oil revenues funneled to the US from Venezuela, The Washington Post reported Thursday.

The Post reported that three senators – Ron Wyden, Elizabeth Warren and Sheldon Whitehouse – directed a letter on the subject to Marco Rubio, the Secretary of State and a key architect of US policy toward Venezuela, and Scott Bessent, the Treasury Secretary.

The senators said that the Trump administration has kept Americans in the dark about where the money is going and what measures – if any – are in place to prevent its misappropriation.

American forces arrested Venezuela’s longtime dictator, Nicolás Maduro, in a surprise night raid back in January. Since then, the US has struck a deal with a new, more pliant regime led by Maduro’s former vice president to route a share of the nation’s oil sales to the US.

Even as the Trump administration seeks to force regime change in Cuba through withering economic isolation, allies of Trump and Marco Rubio, his secretary of state, are angling to get rich off the island’s collapse.

Reporting for The Guardian, Lee Schlenker and Ed Augustin found that business interests connected with Trump and Rubio, the architect of current US designs on Cuba, are jostling to fill the void left by companies squeezed out of the island by the latest barrage of US sanctions.

A pair of Trump-friendly Texas business magnates are fighting to take over a Canadian company’s stake of Cuba’s mineral wealth.

Sources close to the matter say that Trump Organization leaders, operating under a company closely tied to the president’s family, have traveled to Cuba to explore hotel deals after a pair of Spanish hotel chains fled the island.

And Franklin Graham, a close ally of Trump on the evangelical right and head of the evangelical aid organization Samaritan’s Purse, recently won a $40m federal contract to oversee the distribution of humanitarian assistance on the island Trump is pushing toward collapse.

One source with decades of background in Cuba policy put it succinctly: “If I had done during the Biden administration what Trump’s friends have done now, I’d have been put in jail.”

The Trump administration has taken an especially severe stance toward Cuba since the start of Trump’s second term. Rubio, the child of Cuban immigrants, has led that campaign, seeking to bring about his long hoped-for goal of collapsing Cuba’s communist leadership and seeing a new US-friendly government in its place.

The goal of regime change in Cuba has echoes of the Trump administration’s playbook in Venezuela, where Rubio helped orchestrate the toppling of a leftist dictator and the funneling of the country’s oil revenues to US coffers.

Speaking to EU officials in Strasbourg on Thursday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney seemed open to a proposal to grant his country a new “associate member” status within the bloc – even as details remained thin on what, exactly, that would entail.

“We welcome this ambition,” Carney said of the proposal. “Canada and Europe should secure our strategic autonomy through deep cooperation in the full range of strategic capabilities, including critical minerals, defense industrial capacity, AI and compute, energy security, space, and payments.”

Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, first raised the possibility of making Canada an associate member in an address on Wednesday. Her surprise suggestion to grant Canada – notably not in Europe – a heretofore unheard-of special status within the union appeared to catch member states off-guard.

The same was true for President Trump, who slammed the proposal as “laughable” and as a “hostile act” and went on to threaten sweeping tariffs against Europe if it follows through.

Carney tried to articulate what exactly deepened ties between the EU and Canada might look like, saying he was “not ​proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival – only with better manners.”

“We do not seek power to dominate others,” Carney continued. “On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so that ​no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, ​our rule of law.”

The US congresswoman Ilhan Omar is set to introduce a bill that would make federal immigration agencies “pay the price” for terrorising vulnerable communities, blocking nearly $140bn in funding and redirecting it to local recovery efforts, the Guardian has learned.

The Make ICE Pay Act, due to be introduced on Thursday, targets funding previously designated for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) under Donald Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill”.

It would send the money instead to states, local government authorities, nonprofit organisations and small businesses left reeling by Trump’s immigration enforcement crackdowns.

“For over a year, ICE has been tearing through our nation, leading racist terror campaigns that have caused devastating damage to our cities, to our businesses, and to the lives of our constituents,” said Omar, who represents Minnesota’s fifth congressional district, covering the city of Minneapolis and surrounding suburbs.

Beginning last December, thousands of federal immigration agents descended on Minneapolis and surrounding areas, resulting in nearly 4,000 total arrests and the fatal shooting of two US citizens, Renée Good and Alex Pretti. The mood of fear and isolation also had a profound effect on commerce.

Omar added: “In Minneapolis, Operation Metro Surge cost our community nearly $700m. We have a moral responsibility to end this abuse of power. Our bill will force ICE to pay the price for the damage they’ve left in their wake and ensure that these devastating operations can never be repeated.”

A UN fact-finding mission on Iran said it had reasonable grounds to believe the United States was behind two military strikes on a school and sports facility in Iran in ⁠February, and that these constituted war ⁠crimes.

It also found that Iranian ​authorities committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on anti-government protests.

The findings in a new report by the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran, to be submitted to the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, examined the ⁠US’s conduct during the Iran war that began in February and the Iranian government’s response to nationwide unrest that begun in late December.

The Iranian and US permanent missions in Geneva did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.

US officials have previously said military ⁠operations are conducted in accordance with the law of armed conflict, while Iran has consistently rejected allegations of systematic rights violations.

A key Senate Democrat has asked secretary of state Marco Rubio to ensure that US diplomats are involved ⁠in a Pentagon-led review of America’s military presence in Europe that has alarmed Nato allies.

In a letter addressed to Rubio, who is also the ⁠national security advisor, senator Jeanne ⁠Shaheen, the top ​Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, wrote that diplomats, including US ambassadors in potentially affected countries, are being kept out of the loop. The ⁠letter was first shared with Reuters.

The review, which began in June and is due to conclude by the end of the year, is part of a push by ⁠the Trump administration to have Europe rely less on the United States and instead take more responsibility for ​its own defense. The US has around 80,000 ‌troops stationed in Europe.

“The ‌Department of State, which is responsible for managing our bilateral relationships, has traditionally played a substantial role in ‌reviews of this kind,” read the letter.

“Yet what we are hearing through our own conversations, travel across Europe and engagement with our Allies tells a different story. US ambassadors and chiefs of mission in affected countries have been excluded from consultations.“

The unprecedented spate of mid-decade redistricting for the US House has changed the congressional districts for one-tenth of Americans and significantly altered the makeup of at least one-fifth of districts, according to a new study.

A report by Protect Democracy found that 34.8m people - about one in 10 Americans - now live in a different district than they did during the 2024 election cycle.

And about one-fifth of all Americans now live in a district where more than a quarter of voters are new to the district compared with the last election cycle, AP reported.

The findings display the stark overhaul that partisan redistricting fights kicked off by president Donald Trump last year have caused for Americans across the country.

“If this trend continues, it really brings into question whether or not elected officials are really representing their constituents anymore, or if the voters are being randomly picked by mapmakers to squeeze out partisan advantage,” said Ben Raderstorf, a policy advocate at Protect Democracy and one of the paper’s co-authors.

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said the Russia sanctions bill had “so many loopholes” as Congress passed the sweeping bill to give Donald Trump the power to raise tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy.

The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 passed in a 262-159 vote on the last day before Congress goes on recess ahead of the midterm elections. Graham, who died earlier this year, co-authored and submitted the bill more than a year and a half ago.

But Jeffries said the legislation had ​so many loopholes that sanctions harming Russia might not be applied.

“What ​this legislation will do is give Donald Trump, perhaps, unfettered authority to unleash tariffs on the American people,” the New York lawmaker said as he announced he ​would vote no.

double quotation markWhy in the world would this Congress give this president additional authority to visit that kind of economic harm on the American people?

The bill would mandate new sanctions on Russian political and military officials, and foreign networks helping to supply Russia’s war machine and evade existing sanctions. It would also target Russia’s so-called fleet of “shadow tankers”, which have allowed the country to continue to ship crude around the world despite sanctions on its energy exports.

It would also allow Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top purchasers of Russian energy, including China, as well as other countries helping the Kremlin evade sanctions.

Democratic staffers supporting the bill said that it offered a “last chance” to increase sanctions on Russia before Ukraine entered a “long winter”. Russia has improved the drone technology it has used to strike Ukrainian infrastructure as Kyiv has suffered a shortage of anti-air missiles, leaving the country in a dire position.

Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican supporting the bill, called it the US Congress’ “Churchill vs Chamberlain Moment on Russia”.

Donald Trump responded to the Federal Reserve’s unanimous decision on Wednesday to raise its benchmark interest rate by a quarter-percentage point, to a range of 3.75% to 4%, by demanding a massive cut in rates.

Asked why it is so important to him to have his name inscribed on the Kennedy Center, a memorial to another president, Trump said he deserves “recognition” for saving the venue. If not, Trump said, “It’ll end up being ripped down.

Congresswoman Joyce Beatty, a Democrat and Kennedy Center trustee, has filed a motion for an emergency hearing on the performing arts venue’s apparent closure.

Mitch McConnell, the former Republican Senate majority leader who returned to work this week after a months‑long absence, had to be prompted by colleagues as to how to vote near the start of a televised meeting of the Senate agriculture committee on Wednesday.

The House speaker, Mike Johnson, cancelled votes currently scheduled for Thursday, meaning that lower chamber lawmakers will now head back to their districts for the midterm recess a day early. The change to schedule means that the House will avoid voting on Republican congressman Thomas Massie’s resolution to impeach the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth.

Speaking in North Carolina, Trump explicitly compared his effort to blame Democrat Roy Cooper, the former governor and Senate candidate, for the brutal killing of a young Ukrainian refugee, Iryna Zarutska, last year, by using false information, on the infamous 1988 Willie Horton ad.

articles.title: Falcons star Bijan Robinson wants every NFL team to play indoors one day: 'That would be sick'
articles.excerpt: Atlanta Falcons running back Bijan Robinson has a suggestion for the NFL: Why not have all teams play in domes during each season, like he does at Mercedes-Benz Stadium, to let the elements not get in...
articles.body_text:
