Sen. Josh...
articles.body_text:
Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., wants to close a tax loophole that he argued tech giants were using to build data centers in low-income areas, and one that was first passed by Republicans in 2017.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., has indicated that he does not plan to run for president during the 2028 election cycle.

"No, I have no intention of doing so, period," the senator told the Washington Examiner on Tuesday.

Republicans are currently aiming to retain their majorities in the House and Senate during the November 3 midterm elections — but next year, the center of political gravity will likely shift toward the 2028 election cycle, which will include a White House contest with no incumbent.

HAWLEY TAKES AIM AT 'CORPORATE WELFARE' AFTER GOP-BACKED TAX BREAK BOOSTED CONTROVERSIAL INDUSTRY

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., during a Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee confirmation hearing in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"I have no insight to offer you on 2028, one way or another," he said, according to the Examiner. "I don’t know who will run or what will happen. We need to get through these elections first."

Fox News Digital reached out to Hawley's office on Thursday.

THREE NEW COMPANIES FACE JOSH HAWLEY'S INVESTIGATION INTO AI SURVEILLANCE AND VEHICLE TRACKING

President Donald Trump, who is currently serving his second term, is constitutionally barred from election to a third term, leaving the field wide open for 2028 GOP White House hopefuls. But he could potentially choose to endorse a candidate during the 2028 GOP presidential primary.

Hawley, who has served in the Senate since 2019, was re-elected in 2024.

HAWLEY RIPS FLOCK'S SPRAWLING SURVEILLANCE WEB AS TEXAS CITIES CUT CAMERAS OVER PRIVACY AND DATA FEARS

U.S. President Donald Trump pauses as he walks alone along an ivy-covered wall during his final departure from Aras an Uachtarain on Sept. 12, 2026, in Dublin, Ireland. (Artur Widak/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Hawley emphasized the importance of conservative religious voters, describing them as "the backbone of this party," according to the Examiner.

"You cannot win anything without them. You cannot win a primary without them. You cannot win a general election without them. And I would caution anybody who thinks that you can do without them in our voting coalition — you will have a voting coalition of like 10% without religious conservatives, without evangelical Protestants, without conservative Catholics, without conservative Orthodox Jews. So, I’d be real careful about trying to marginalize that coalition," he said, according to the outlet.

Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: NBA star Irving pledges to pay Al-Shaair’s NFL fine over Hind Rajab message
articles.excerpt: Basketball superstar Kyrie Irving has offered to pay a fine for American football player Azeez Al-Shaair, who was penalised for wearing the name of Hind Rajab, a Palestinian girl killed by Israeli for...
articles.body_text:
Basketball superstar Kyrie Irving has offered to pay a fine for American football player Azeez Al-Shaair, who was penalised for wearing the name of Hind Rajab, a Palestinian girl killed by Israeli forces in Gaza.

Al-Shaair was handed a fine of $11,941 by the National Football League (NFL) on Wednesday as he was found to be in breach of the NFL’s rules on players’ equipment and clothing during his team Houston Texans’ game against the Buffalo Bills last weekend.

Shortly after the fine was announced by an NFL reporter on X, the pro-Palestine basketball player responded to the tweet by saying he would “take care” of it.

Al-Shaair, 29, is a linebacker for the Houston-based NFL team and a vocal advocate for Palestinian rights.

During his team’s last NFL game, Al-Shaair wrote Rajab’s name on his eye black, a sticker or paint frequently used by NFL players to reduce glare.

Five-year-old Rajab was killed in Gaza after Israeli soldiers opened fire on her family’s stranded car. A phone call by the Palestinian Red Crescent documented her final moments and was the subject of an Oscar-nominated docudrama.

Al-Shaair, a Black American Muslim player, has frequently spoken about the plight of Palestinians and has paid the price for it.

He was also fined in January, during the NFL’s last season, when he displayed the message “Stop The Genocide” on his nose tape. While it did not specifically refer to a particular conflict, it was widely understood to be about Gaza and Sudan.

The NFL’s fine on Al-Shaair comes at a time when Robert Kraft, the owner of the Boston-based team New England Patriots, confirmed that he pressured pop star Ed Sheeran to drop rapper Macklemore from his tour of the United States.

The billionaire is the owner of Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, one of the venues where Macklemore was due to appear on stage as the opening act for Sheeran’s US tour in late September.

Letting Macklemore perform in Gillette Stadium would, Kraft said, cross a line, as he described the rapper’s recent performances as including a “broader history of anti-Semitic rhetoric and imagery”.

Kraft is known for launching a so-called “anti-Semitic campaign” during Israel’s genocide in Gaza in 2023, when players, coaches and executives from his Patriots team wore blue pins.

On October 15, 2023, the NFL observed a moment of silence for Israel during a game between the Baltimore Ravens and the Tennessee Titans in London, United Kingdom, while the league has sanctioned its player for raising awareness for Palestinians.

The NFL was criticised on social media for slapping a fine on Al-Shaair, with one user calling the move “inhumane”.

“He is advocating for the murder of this innocent child Hind Rajab in Palestine and they fine him?! Nah, that is so inhumane. You should be ashamed of yourself,” the user wrote.

Prominent American Muslim scholar Omar Suleiman questioned whether Al-Shaair would have faced a similar punishment if his tape carried the name of Holocaust victim Anne Frank instead.

“Why is honoring murdered Palestinian children ‘an unauthorized message’?” he asked in a post on X.

Meanwhile, the Texas chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations backed Al-Shaair over his continued advocacy for Palestinians.

“We commend Al-Shaair for using his platform to highlight the memory of Hind Rajab, one of the many children murdered by the Israeli government during its genocide in Gaza,” the rights group said in a statement on its website.

“The NFL has no problem with coaches wearing pins developed for genocide supporter Robert Kraft’s “Stand Up to Jewish Hate” campaign, and it should have no problem with an NFL player mentioning the name of a girl killed in that genocide,” the statement went on to add.

“Al-Shaair’s message was rooted in basic human decency and concern for innocent lives. That should not be controversial, much less subject to a fine.”

Meanwhile, nine-time National Basketball Association (NBA) All-Star Irving has previously made his pro-Palestine stance on Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza clear.

In February, Irving wore a shirt reading “PRESS” at the NBA All-Star Game to honour journalists who had been killed in Gaza while covering the war.

According to reports, the tag on his shirt read: “Dedicated to our beloved journalists in Gaza showing the world the truth.”

In April, Irving changed his display picture on Instagram to an image of a Palestinian child blocked from attending school by Israeli soldiers in the occupied West Bank.

During a pre-game interview in 2024, he was seen wearing a chain with the Palestine flag in the shape of Israel’s landmass.

In 2023, the basketball player wore a keffiyeh, a cotton headdress with a distinctive checkered pattern worn in many parts of the Arab world that represents Palestinian identity, during a post-match news conference.

articles.title: Tories challenge chancellor to rule out tax rises in budget as Badenoch labelled ‘embarrassment’ for Bank of England gaffe – UK politics live
articles.excerpt:
The Conservatives want to brand Burnham’s administration as a ‘traditional tax and spend socialist government’

Good morning. With less than six weeks so go until the budget, economics is rising up th...
articles.body_text:
The Conservatives want to brand Burnham’s administration as a ‘traditional tax and spend socialist government’

Good morning. With less than six weeks so go until the budget, economics is rising up the agenda at Westminster. The Bank of England is announcing its latest interest rate decision later – Graeme Wearden will have all the details on his business live blog – and Andrew Griffith is giving his first major speech since being appointed as shadow chancellor just over two weeks ago.

Not surprisingly, Griffith is urging the chancellor, John Healey, to rule out tax rises in the budget. He has been doing interviews this morning and he told BBC Breakfast:

double quotation markThe taxes or the fear of taxes … are driving really big taxpayers to leave our country for overseas, taking hundreds of millions of pounds of tax revenues that will pay for public services …

The thing that they (the government) could do right now is take off the table the fears of ordinary small businesses, the self-employed, who are getting up now, going to work, and allow them to get on with their lives with confidence that the taxes are not going to go up.

The speech will focus on small businesses, and Griffith will announce that he has appointed two advisers – the Tory peer and former MP Craig Mackinlay, a chartered accountant, and Robert Colvile, the outgoing head of the Centre for Policy Studies thinktank – to produce a report for him on cutting red tape for business.

The Tories are keen to present Burnham’s administration as what Andy Haldane would call just another “traditional tax and spend socialist government” and yesterday Kemi Badenoch leapt on what she thought was new evidence to confirm this theory. She posted this on social media.

double quotation markOnly one party has ever rescued the country from trade union control. We’re ready to do so again.

If you weren’t sure what kind of Labour government we have, or want to know what’s in store for you and your family finances, the news below is a big clue and it’s not good news 👇

She was responding to a tweet from the Sun saying Paul Nowak has been made a director at the Bank of England.

It was true; he has. There are up to 14 directors on the Bank’s court of directors and Nowak, general secretary of the TUC, has been appointed as one of its non-executive directors. The court is not the body that sets interest rates; it just oversees the Bank’s administration.

But there is nothing very new or surprising (or socialist) about this. Nowak is replacing Frances O’Grady, who was also TUC general secretary. She was made a non-executive director at the Bank under a Tory government. As was her TUC predecessor.

In fact, this has been happening for decades. Rupert Harrison, who was chief of staff to George Osborne when he was chancellor, took to X yesterday to suggest to his Tory colleagues that they keep things in perspective.

double quotation markGot no take on this particular candidate but worth noting that it’s been a tradition to have a trade union representative on the Court of the Bank for decades. Since the War I think.

9.30am: The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government publishes figures on local government spending.

11am: Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, delivers his speech.

Noon: The Bank of England announces its interest rate decision.

Jonathan Powell, the national security adviser, told Andy Burnham and Ed Miliband that the government should delay banning trade with illegal settlements on the West Bank until after the Israeli elections, Tim Shipman says in a report for this week’s Spectator. He suggests this advice was ignored in part because Labour wanted to announce the decision before the Holborn and St Pancras byelection.

double quotation markThe truth is that Burnham and Miliband ignored the advice they were given – which was that if they were determined to sanction Israel, they should not do so before the Israeli election on 27 October.

It may not be surprising that this was the message from the Israeli foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, when Miliband called him on 11 August to warn sanctions were imminent. ‘He said postpone it until after the elections,’ a diplomatic source confirms. It was also the message the Israeli embassy in London – and its new chargé d’affaires Chris Cantor – was relaying to the Foreign Office. ‘Their message was clear: why do it now? Wait until after the elections, because something might change,’ a senior Labour figure says.

The British ambassador in Tel Aviv, Simon Walters, who was of the same opinion, delivered a ‘very explicit’ warning not to move so quickly. As a former director of national security for the Middle East in the Foreign Office, he had a deep understanding of the security implications. More remarkably, Jonathan Powell, the National Security Adviser, was of the same view. He was the most important figure in government on foreign policy during Keir Starmer’s premiership, but now seems to have been ignored on the first major issue of Burnham’s tenure.

Shipman says the government has defended announcing the decision before the Israeli elections on the grounds that “tenders to build 1,200 homes on a settlement site called E1, an action seen as an impediment to a two-state solution, were due by 19 October.”

Labour won’t let Andrew Griffith forget Liz Truss. This is what it said overnight in response to the trail of Griffith’s speech.

double quotation markWe won’t take any lectures from the Tories on the economy - not least when it was only last week that Andrew Griffith was praising the “lots of good things” in Liz Truss’s disastrous mini-budget.

Robert Jenrick, who served with Griffith in the last Tory government and who is now Reform UK’s Treasury spokesperson, also issued a “pre-buttal” ahead of Griffith’s speech. Jenrick said:

double quotation markAndrew Griffith was the very person who abolished the Office for Tax Simplification after the tax code ballooned to 23,000 pages - why on earth would anyone believe him now? After making IR35 worse, freezing VAT thresholds and imposing reams of red tape, businesses won’t forget the Tories’ betrayal.

In a news release issued ahead of his speech this morning, Andrew Griffith, the new shadow chancellor, gave details of some of the questions he wants the experts he has asked to review small business regulation to address. (See 8.58am.) He said:

double quotation mark[Craig Mackinlay and Robert Colvile] will produce a report taking evidence from small business and self-employed organisations. While they will have a wide remit, they will consider in particular these key questions, and report in December:

-Why have past attempts to reduce the regulatory and compliance burden on small business and the self-employed failed, and what specifically should be done to reduce the burden successfully?

-Where is HMRC’s performance falling short and what specifically should be done to improve it?

-Where do the worst complexities in filing returns and claiming the reliefs small businesses are entitled to sit?

-Where did the 2017 and 2021 reforms to off-payroll working, known as IR35, go too far, and what should a new, better framework look like to cut compliance costs and preserve flexibility while guarding against abuse?

-What are the best systems for small business and the self-employed in use around the world?

Kemi Badenoch was not the only person who criticised the government’s decision to appoint Paul Nowak to the Bank of England’s court, in line with a long tradition that the TUC gets representation there. (See 8.58am and 9.24am.) Last night Richard Tice, the Reform UK deputy leader, issued this statement.

double quotation markThis is staggering. Our socialist Chancellor has dished out a big Bank of England finance job to a socialist union boss who knows nothing about finance.

Clearly, trade union donations not only buy your way into government policymaking, but also onto the Bank of England’s board. This is cronyism in plain sight.

The government should stop talking about “net zero” when talking about the transition to clean energy because the phrase has become “a distraction”, MPs say.

The cross-party Commons energy committee says the phrase has “lost much of its significant positive association” amid increasing misinformation.

double quotation markThe term net zero has become a distraction from the broader aims and the benefits of the energy transition and the politics of the energy transition have become mired in a stale debate on the cost and feasibility of achieving an emissions target. The public debate fails to reflect the wider benefits of engaging with the transition or the costs of not tackling climate change …

Future government communications under the new administration should be more demonstrably relevant to people’s lives, with clear information on how people might reduce their costs or minimise their exposure to future costs in a way that they believe they can achieve. The department should drop ‘net zero’ from its name as a start to making its communications less technocratic and reduce its use in regular communications and public statements, instead focussing on wider societal benefits.

The full name of the committee is the energy security and net zero committee, which mirrors the full name of the government’s energy department. The committee says that should change.

The Conservatives and Reform UK have both strongly criticised the government’s net zero policies, using the label as a catch-all phrase to cover what in effect are multiple policies to promote the switch from fossil fuels to renewables. Richard Tice, the Reform UK deputy leader, likes talking about “net stupid zero”, although his slogan has not been widely adopted.

When Theresa May was PM, she passed legislation committing the UK to reducing carbon emissions to net zero by 2050 and at the time there was cross-party consensus on this being a good target. But under Kemi Badenoch’s leadership the Tories have abandoned support for this; Reform UK was never signed up in the first place.

In an interview this morning, Martin McCluskey, an energy minister, told Times Radio he did not agree with the committee’s claim that “net zero” has now become a negative term.

double quotation markIt’s not just about tackling climate change, which is really important, and we need to carry on doing that. But it’s also about making our whole energy system more secure and making sure that our national security is protected as well.

The UK should introduce a ban on almost all gambling advertising to protect public health, a cross-party group of peers has urged, prompting fury from the lobby group for bookmakers and casinos. Rob Davies has the story.

This is from Torsten Bell, a Treasury minister, on Kemi Badenoch’s attack on Paul Nowak getting a post as a non-executive director on the Bank of England’s court.

double quotation markTwo Conservative Chancellors appointed Frances O’Grady - then TUC general secretary - to two terms on the Court of the Bank in the recent past. As @rbrharrison the welcome appointment of @nowak_paul today has a LOT of precedents

And the Labour MP Yuan Yang, a former FT journalist, has posted a thread on social media explaining the role of the Bank’s court.

Chris Bryant, the Northern Ireland secretary, has described Kemi Badenoch as “an embarrassment” over her attack on Paul Nowak’s appointment to the Bank of England’s court.

articles.title: At least 19 injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine
articles.excerpt:
Ukrainian officials say at least 19 people have been injured in Russian missile and drone strikes targeting Kyiv and surrounding areas.

Ukraine’s Air Force said on Thursday that it destroyed or suppr...
articles.body_text:
Ukrainian officials say at least 19 people have been injured in Russian missile and drone strikes targeting Kyiv and surrounding areas.

Ukraine’s Air Force said on Thursday that it destroyed or suppressed 131 Russian aerial targets during the overnight attacks, adding that the main areas targeted were the Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia and Odesa regions.

Strikes were recorded at 36 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at five sites.

Russia’s Defence Ministry said its forces hit metallurgical and electronics plants, factories of the military-industrial complex, energy and transport facilities in the three regions.

Three bulk carriers and a ferry used to carry supplies for the Ukrainian military were hit in the port of Chornomorsk, added the ministry.

In Odesa, seven people were injured, including two children, according to Ukraine’s State Emergency Service. High-rise apartments in a residential building were damaged.

A private residential building in Odesa was destroyed, while warehouses, a nursery school, cars and garages were damaged at other locations, the service said on Telegram.

In Kyiv’s Dniprovsky district, a warehouse, office building, residential buildings and cars were damaged, according to local authorities. A warehouse was damaged in the Solomyansky district, while a warehouse and cars were damaged in the Darnitsky district.

In the Podilsky district, the roof of a non-residential building was damaged, authorities said.

In the Kyiv region, civilian areas and infrastructure were targeted in the Obukhiv, Brovary, Fastiv and Bucha districts, according to Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Regional Administration.

A total of 33 sites were damaged, with the worst reported in the Brovary district, where 14 sites were hit, and the Fastiv district, where 10 were damaged, Tkachenko said in a statement on Telegram.

The damaged sites included homes, warehouses, production facilities and vehicles. No casualties or injuries were reported, he said.

Al Jazeera’s Rory Challands, reporting from Kyiv, said the strikes come days after United States President Donald Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to suspend attacks on energy facilities.

“We have a situation where just a few days ago, [US President] Donald Trump announced that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop hitting each other’s energy targets,” as Trump has blamed the Russia-Ukraine war for the rising cost of diesel around the world, said Challands.

However, “neither Russia nor Ukraine have agreed to this and they are continuing to hit each other’s energy targets”, said Challands, with Russia promising to increase its “mass attacks on the Ukrainian energy grid going into the winter months”.

Russian attacks “almost collapsed the Ukrainian energy grid” last winter, with Ukraine’s energy providers now saying that they are “expecting another very tough winter” but hoping that it will be better than the previous one, said Challands.

A Ukrainian drone attack hit an oil refinery in the Russian city of Yaroslavl, northeast of Moscow, said President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

The resulting fire from the attack had been extinguished, announced regional governor Mikhail Yevrayev.

Zelenskyy also reported damage to Russian warplanes and helicopters in a strike on a military base in the southern city of Rostov.

“There have also been good results in the Black Sea,” the president said on social media, without giving further details.

articles.title: Beckham backs Messi for Ballon d’Or after netting 100th Inter Miami goal
articles.excerpt:
Lionel Messi has been backed for a record ninth Ballon d’Or by former England captain David Beckham, weeks after the Argentinian icon announced his international retirement.

The 39-year-old scored hi...
articles.body_text:
Lionel Messi has been backed for a record ninth Ballon d’Or by former England captain David Beckham, weeks after the Argentinian icon announced his international retirement.

The 39-year-old scored his 100th goal for Inter Miami, co-owned by Beckham, on Wednesday as the Florida-based side won the Campeones Cup by beating Cruz Azul 2-0 in the annual clash between Major League Soccer and Mexican Liga MX champions.

It was Inter Miami’s first Campeones Cup triumph and was sealed for the reigning MLS Cup winners by a late Messi corner that was headed home by Casemiro to seal the win.

Victory marked Messi’s first trophy of the year, two months after the heartbreak of losing the FIFA World Cup 2026 final to Spain with Argentina.

After the game, Beckham, who played for both Manchester United and Real Madrid before joining MLS side LA Galaxy, led the praise for Messi.

“When you see him do things like this tonight, when you see him have the World Cup that he’s had … there is no one at 39 that’s doing that, and doing it at that level,” said Beckham.

“So he deserves to be considered for the Ballon d’Or. In my opinion, he should win it.”

Brazil international Casemiro, who joined Inter Miami from Manchester United in the summer, also paid tribute to his illustrious teammate Messi.

“We have to enjoy this because we don’t know how long we’ll have it,” Casemiro said.

“What he has done and continues to do for football is incredible … he remains the best. He proved it at the World Cup and continues to prove it in MLS.”

Cruz Azul had the game’s first big chance, Jose Paradela’s shot saved at the near post by Miami goalkeeper Dayne St Clair.

Miami’s opener came in the 24th minute. Though the goalscorer was no surprise, it was a rare Messi header that broke the deadlock.

Luis Suarez crossed from the byline, and the 5-foot-7 Messi outjumped Willer Ditta with a diving header to give Miami the lead.

Suarez nearly turned provider again in the 32nd minute. He received a sumptuous cross-field ball from Messi and scooped it up for German Berterame, whose dinked effort was cleared off the line.

Early in the second half, Messi appeared to have scored his 101st Miami goal, racing through one-on-one from a Suarez through ball and placing his shot in off the post, but was ruled offside.

Cruz Azul should have equalised in the 67th minute, but substitute Gabriel Fernandez’s glancing header hit the post, and Casemiro blocked the follow-up shot.

A Messi corner gave Miami the two-goal cushion, finding Casemiro, who nodded the ball low to the far post in the 81st minute.

St Clair denied Cruz Azul a late consolation, saving well from a Paradela free kick.

The trophy came in new Inter Miami head coach Cristian “Kily” Gonzalez’s first game in charge.

Argentine manager Gonzalez was appointed last month, but due to visa delays only took his first training sessions this week.

The annual Campeones Cup pits the previous year’s MLS Cup winner against the winner of Mexico’s Campeon de Campeones.

It was the eighth edition of the cup, which is always hosted by the MLS participant.

Mexican teams had won the three most recent editions before Miami’s victory on Wednesday.

Mexican giants Cruz Azul have still never won the Campeones Cup. They lost the 2021 final.

The World Cup final defeat will not be Messi’s last for Argentina after it was announced that he will play in the South Americans’ friendly against Benin on October 6.

Messi’s eight Ballon d’Or titles stand three clear of Portugal’s Cristiano Ronaldo, and five clear of France’s Michel Platini and Dutch pair, Johan Cruyff and Marco van Basten.

articles.title: Man says meat-only 'lion diet' cleared psoriasis covering 90% of his body, ended decades of depression
articles.excerpt: Florida resident Stephen Lashbrook recounts living with extensive psoriasis, debilitating joint discomfort and depression before adopting an extremely restrictive meat-centric eating regimen that he s...
articles.body_text:
Florida resident Stephen Lashbrook recounts living with extensive psoriasis, debilitating joint discomfort and depression before adopting an extremely restrictive meat-centric eating regimen that he says changed his life.

A 50-year-old Florida man who says he spent decades battling severe psoriasis, pain and depression credits an extreme "lion diet" with saving his life.

Stephen Lashbrook, of Pensacola, told Fox News Digital that his depression began at just 4 years old. In his teens, it was compounded by chronic pain, sleeplessness and, in his early 20s, he was diagnosed with psoriasis, an immune-mediated skin disease.

"I was probably 90% covered in psoriasis," Lashbrook said. "My body was just one big, giant, itchy, flaky scab."

DOCTORS DIVIDED OVER NEW DIET TREND THAT HAS BABIES LICKING BUTTER AND GUMMING RIBEYE STEAK

Creams, steroids and other medications did not help, he said. Doctors recommended expensive, long-term injections to combat his inflammation, which left Lashbrook feeling hopeless and suicidal.

Stephen Lashbrook says he struggled for decades with psoriasis, chronic pain and depression before changing his diet. (Stephen Lashbrook)

Then, he came across a TED Talk from Mikhaila Peterson, an influencer and the daughter of Canadian psychologist and author Jordan Peterson, who used a meat-only elimination diet to tackle her own health issues.

"It gave me a whole new lease on life," he said.

RED MEAT CAN HELP YOUR MOOD IF PART OF A HEALTHY, BALANCED DIET, STUDY SUGGESTS

Lashbrook said he initially cut sugar, grains, fruits and vegetables from his diet.

On Jan. 1, 2024, he committed to the "lion diet," a strict carnivore diet variation centered on ruminant animal meat, "your cow, your buffalo, your lamb, your goat," he told Fox News Digital.

Stephen Lashbrook says a meat-only diet helped him manage symptoms he experienced for decades. (Stephen Lashbrook)

Within a week, Lashbrook said his itching and suicidal thoughts stopped and, within a month, his skin began to clear up and his pain subsided.

"I haven't had one suicidal thought. I haven't had any depression. I haven't had any pain," he said. "All my skin issues cleared up."

RFK JR. CLAIMS HE LOST 20 POUNDS IN 20 DAYS, GAINED MENTAL CLARITY ON EXTREME DIET

His current menu consists of only grass-fed ground beef and steak.

Lashbrook said he generally eats one meal per day — about 1½ to 2 pounds of high-fat ground beef usually cooked in an air fryer.

After years of pain and severe psoriasis symptoms, Lashbrook adopted a strict all-beef "lion diet," he told Fox News Digital. (Courtesy Stephen Lashbrook)

"I feel like I'm reverse aging," he said.

DOCTORS IN TRAINING LEARN COOKING SKILLS TO HELP PATIENTS AMID AMERICA'S CHRONIC DISEASE CRISIS

His reported improvements are based on personal experience. Lashbrook said he has not had follow-up blood work or visited a doctor since changing his diet, preferring to judge the approach by how he feels.

"Everyone's different," he added. "Not everybody needs to be on a lion diet. ... I'm a very specific case."

Lashbrook generally eats one high-fat beef meal per day, he told Fox News Digital. (iStock)

Dr. Michael Aziz, a New York City-based internist and regenerative medicine specialist, said that while some people may feel better after cutting sugar and ultra-processed foods, that does not establish the carnivore diet as a treatment for psoriasis or other chronic conditions.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"Many people judge this diet by their success, by their weight loss, but they don't look long-term at their lifespan, how it can be affected by those diets," he told Fox News Digital.

"If people don't hear that these healings are possible, they're not going to know."

One of the main problems, Aziz added, is that carnivore-centered diets lack fiber.

"They can lead to problems like constipation. They can lead to kidney stones. They can lead to increased risks for heart attack and stroke," he said.

Yet meat and protein-forward have drawn recent attention online and in the mainstream, especially as people seek to cut out ultra-processed foods.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has said he follows a carnivore diet centered on meat and fermented foods, claiming it helped him lose weight and gain mental clarity.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has said he follows a carnivore diet centered on meat and fermented foods. (United States Department of Health and Human Services)

Like Lashbrook, Kennedy has acknowledged that his experience may not be right for everyone and medical experts have cautioned that long-term effects of the carnivore diet remain unclear.

Lashbrook will share his story this week at Carni-Con, a virtual convention centered around carnivore diets. The event runs from Sept. 18–20 and features doctors, creators and other diet advocates.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"The stories are what's most important," Lashbrook said.

"If people don't hear that these healings are possible, they're not going to know."

Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

articles.title: ‘We live with a big burden’: US sexual abuse survivor hopes priest’s death brings closure
articles.excerpt:
Keith Townsend says he hopes death of Ronald Paquin in prison helps victims and families to ‘keep pressing forward’

A survivor of childhood sexual abuse by a defrocked Boston Catholic priest who was ...
articles.body_text:
Keith Townsend says he hopes death of Ronald Paquin in prison helps victims and families to ‘keep pressing forward’

A survivor of childhood sexual abuse by a defrocked Boston Catholic priest who was portrayed admitting to molesting minors in the Oscar-winning Hollywood film Spotlight says he hopes the clergyman’s recent death in prison helps victims of his crimes and their families “keep pressing forward every single day”.

“We live with a big burden in our hearts and on our backs,” Keith Townsend said on Wednesday while reflecting on the criminal charges which he successfully pursued against Ronald Paquin, who was imprisoned in 2019 and died in custody at age 83 on 11 September. “And my hope is that people can find closure and move on.”

Those remarks by Townsend, 52, during a telephone interview were a notable reaction to the death of one of the key figures in the clergy sexual abuse and cover-up scandal with the Catholic archdiocese of Boston that – among other consequences – prompted the resignation of the institution’s archbishop, Bernard Law, at the end of 2002, as well as policy reforms across the US church.

That same year, Paquin had pleaded guilty to sexually abusing an altar server from 1989 to 1992 while working at St John the Baptist church in the Boston suburb of Haverhill, Massachusetts. He was stripped of his clerical status and imprisoned in Massachusetts for that abuse, which was first publicly exposed in a Pulitzer-winning series of investigative articles by the Boston Globe newspaper’s Spotlight team.

Paquin was freed in 2015. And learning of that release motivated Townsend – once a St John altar server, too – to come forward and report being abused himself by Paquin while on camping trips to Kennebunkport, Maine, between 1985 and 1989.

As Townsend put it, he was between the ages of eight and 13 when Paquin molested him. Townsend recalled Paquin plying him with drugs and alcohol during the abuse, eventually leading him to battles with substance abuse addiction and incarceration.

A Maine grand jury indicted Paquin in 2017 on new charges of gross sexual misconduct in connection with Townsend and another individual. Paquin faced a jury trial in November 2018 which culminated in a guilty verdict against him with regards to Townsend, though he was acquitted of having abused the other individual.

Maine judge Wayne Douglas sentenced Paquin in May 2019 to 16 more years in prison. Paquin was in the Mountain View correctional facility in Charleston, Maine, when he died, the state’s department of correction said in a news release.

Speaking five days later, Townsend said he first got word of Paquin’s death from his wife, who saw it circulating on the news and social media. He said he understood the many reactions which he subsequently heard or read that took delight in news of Paquin’s death.

But Townsend, now a New Hampshire resident, also said he used the occasion to think about his “shaking off” the drug and alcohol addiction which had a grip on him in the wake of Paquin’s abuse. He said he contemplated the family he had built after overcoming “one of the biggest obstacles that could be thrown” at a person.

“I get those who think the attitude should be, ‘Fuck him. Fuck what he did to me,’” Townsend said. “But look where I am today.”

Townsend said he sought Paquin’s re-imprisonment with the aim of “protecting children … not [from] a man [but] a monster”.

“Massachusetts just kind of let him go,” Townsend said. “So I had to dig deep … [because] I didn’t want anybody else to possibly have to go through [his] abuse. Maine thankfully had the balls to take this case, aggressively prosecute it and get a good outcome.”

Townsend said he had not yet been able to see Spotlight, which dramatizes the Globe’s uncovering of the clergy sexual abuse scandal that roiled the city’s archdiocese. And therefore Townsend had not viewed the famous scene in the film in which Rachel McAdams, playing reporter Sacha Pfeiffer, confronts an actor portraying Paquin on his home’s front doorstep about allegations of molesting boys at St John the Baptist.

“Sure, I fooled around – but I never felt gratified myself,” the actor playing Paquin, Richard O’Rourke, says in response as the journalist scribbles notes in a paper pad while wearing an astonished facial expression.

“Right, um, but you admit to molesting boys at St John the Baptist?” McAdams’ Pfeiffer then asks O’Rourke’s Paquin. The latter’s reply: “Yes, yes. But, as I said, I never got any pleasure from it.”

Another person closely familiar with Spotlight offered an opinion of that scene’s legacy on Wednesday.

Attorney Mitchell Garabedian – who is portrayed in the 2015 movie by Stanley Tucci and has represented numerous victims of sexual abuse by Paquin and other clerics – said that part of Spotlight provided a powerful cue to survivors of clergy molesters that they were not alone.

“It gave a sense of, ‘A-ha, I’m not the only one,’” in one of Hollywood’s most critically acclaimed films, Garabedian said. ‘“It wasn’t my fault, and I shouldn’t feel guilty.’”

Townsend said ultimately he is grateful for anything that raised awareness about Paquin’s atrocities before his push to bring him to justice.

“When I lay my head down tonight, I know it saved lives” getting Paquin imprisoned for his remaining years, Townsend added. “And that’s what matters to me.”

articles.title: Memphis mom says Trump brought peace to streets as Democratic DA battles task force oversight
articles.excerpt:
Memphis mother Dalisia Ballinger credits President Trump’s crime crackdown with silencing gunfire in her neighborhood and sounds off on the growing transparency battle surrounding task force cases.

A...
articles.body_text:
Memphis mother Dalisia Ballinger credits President Trump’s crime crackdown with silencing gunfire in her neighborhood and sounds off on the growing transparency battle surrounding task force cases.

A Memphis mother says President Donald Trump’s federal crime crackdown silenced the gunfire that years of pleas to local leaders could not and finally allowed her children to play outside.

"For once, I’m walking to my mailbox and it’s quiet," Dalisia Ballinger told Fox News Digital. "I’m hearing the birds chirp. I’m hearing the birds sing. I’m seeing children play in the middle of the street. I’m seeing fathers playing football."

The striking turnaround turned Ballinger, a former journalist and violent-crime victim, into one of the most outspoken supporters of the Memphis Safe Task Force as the operation marks one year on the ground.

It also put her at the center of a growing clash with Shelby County District Attorney Steve Mulroy, a Democrat whose lawsuit against two new state oversight laws has sparked a petition demanding that he abandon the legal fight and disclose how his office handles cases generated by the task force.

FORMER CHICAGO DETECTIVE SAYS ONE CITY'S MURDER PLUNGE OFFERS WINDY CITY CRIME BLUEPRIN

A Memphis Police Department officer, right, patrols with members of the National Guard, Friday, Oct. 10, 2025, in Memphis, Tenn. (George Walker IV/AP Photo)

"Public safety should not be up for debate," Ballinger said. "I don’t care if you are a Republican. I don’t care if you are a Democrat."

Trump established the multi-agency operation through a presidential memorandum on Sept. 15, 2025, ordering federal, state and local authorities to coordinate against street and violent crime in Memphis. The task force is led by the U.S. Marshals Service and includes mobilized members of the Tennessee National Guard.

The White House said Tuesday that the operation had produced 12,747 arrests as of Sept. 15, including 131 homicide arrests, 1,276 firearms arrests and 1,408 arrests of known gang members.

The administration also credited the task force with taking 2,160 illegal guns off the streets and recovering 189 missing children.

FBI ANNOUNCES 305 ARRESTS, 24 MISSING CHILDREN RECOVERED IN CHICAGO DURING OPERATION NEW DAWN

President Donald Trump speaks during an event to sign a memorandum to send federal resources to Memphis, Tennessee, for a surge against local crime, in the Oval Office at the White House in Washington, D.C., on September 15, 2025. (Jonathan Ernst/Reuters)

Overall crime in Memphis fell nearly 36% compared with the previous year, while murders dropped 36%, robberies fell 42% and vehicle thefts plunged 57%, according to figures released by the White House. City data had already shown crime falling before the task force arrived, and the statistics do not establish how much of the decline resulted directly from the federal surge.

"That era is over. President Trump rejected the excuses, restored law and order, and once again proved that decline is a choice," the White House said.

FBI REPORTS LARGEST DROP IN VIOLENT CRIME AND MURDER SINCE 1937 AS HOMICIDES FALL MORE THAN 18%

Ballinger said the change became personal when her children could play outdoors without the constant fear that had gripped her neighborhood.

She recalled a shooting four houses away in which she said roughly 30 gunshots struck a home occupied by a grandmother and her grandchildren. The family never returned, she said, leaving the property overtaken by grass and weeds.

TRUMP'S DC CRIME CRACKDOWN 'WORKING' AS CITY SEES HOMICIDES PLUMMET 43% SINCE 2025: SLAIN INTERN'S MOM

"We’ve been begging for years for our local leaders for assistance and for help," Ballinger said. "My children deserve peace, and with the Memphis Safe Task Force being here, we’ve finally been able to get that peace."

Now, she and other supporters argue the operation’s arrests mean little if prosecutors later reduce or dismiss cases without explaining why.

PROSECUTOR OUSTED AFTER ALLEGED ROMANCE WITH ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT SEX-CRIME SUSPECT: 'PATTERN OF MISCONDUCT'

Federal law enforcement officers stand at the intersection of Beale St. and N. Second St., Wednesday, Oct. 8, 2025, in Memphis. (George Walker IV/AP Photo)

A Change.org petition titled "Stop Memphis DA From Protecting Criminals" had gathered nearly 10,000 verified signatures Wednesday.

The petition calls on Mulroy to drop a May lawsuit challenging the Memphis Safe Task Force Accountability Act and a separate law that authorizes the Tennessee attorney general to audit his office’s decisions in task force cases.

The accountability law requires Mulroy’s office to submit a report every 10 business days when it settles or dismisses a charge arising from the task force. The second law allows the state attorney general to review prosecutorial decisions in those cases and ask the Tennessee Supreme Court to appoint a temporary prosecutor.

PRIMARY SHOWDOWN: CONSERVATIVE FIREBRAND MARSHA BLACKBURN EYES GOVERNOR'S OFFICE IN TENNESSEE

Shelby County District Attorney Steve Mulroy is challenging two Tennessee laws that increase oversight of his office’s handling of Memphis Safe Task Force cases. (Fox News Digital)

Mulroy argues that both laws unconstitutionally single out Shelby County, intrude on the discretion of a locally elected prosecutor and burden his staff with duplicative reporting. His office said it already reports case outcomes under existing Tennessee law.

"These bills target Shelby County unfairly and infringe on the rights of Shelby County voters," Mulroy said when the lawsuit was filed. He has characterized the dispute as a battle over whether Shelby County voters or state officials in Nashville control the district attorney’s office.

Petition supporters see the lawsuit differently.

"Thanks to President Trump, the Memphis Safe Task Force has delivered more for this city in one year than anyone thought possible," Ballinger, one of the petition's leading voices, said in a statement. "While federal, state, and local agents risk their lives taking criminals off our streets, DA Mulroy is fighting in court to hide how his office is undermining this task force."

President Donald Trump arrives to participate in a roundtable discussion on public safety at a Tennessee Air National Guard Base, Monday, March 23, 2026, in Memphis. (Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo)

U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., and Tennessee state Sen. Brent Taylor previously pressed  Mulroy for details after his office reported that 430 of 514 felony cases resolved in December 2025 ended without prison time and that 166 of the cases were categorized as violent. The lawmakers said the figures left unanswered how many defendants in violent cases received no prison sentence. Mulroy has accused his Republican critics of distorting crime data for political purposes.

Ballinger rejected the claim that the petition is merely a partisan campaign against a Democratic prosecutor.

"We have children. We have regular people that might not even be into politics," she said. "We deserve peace. Whether it’s on the East Coast, the West Coast or South, we all deserve peace."

MISSISSIPPI DISTRICT ATTORNEY JODY OWENS RESIGNS AFTER PLEADING GUILTY IN FEDERAL BRIBERY CASE: REPORT

Some Memphis residents think the police department, Tennessee Highway Patrol troopers and FBI are effectively fighting crime. (Fox News)

The task force has also drawn fierce opposition. The ACLU of Tennessee and several Memphis residents have accused agents of aggressive policing and retaliation against people who record law enforcement.

Four residents filed a federal lawsuit this year alleging harassment, unlawful arrests and physical mistreatment while exercising their First Amendment rights.

The allegations have not been proven in court, while task force supporters point to thousands of arrests and sharply falling crime numbers as evidence the operation is working.

Ballinger said legitimate complaints should be reviewed, but she does not believe they justify dismantling an operation she credits with making her neighborhood livable again.

"I’m all for fairness, and I’m all for law and order," she said. "If we need to go back to the table [and] restructure so that people can feel safe, we can definitely put that on the board."

For Ballinger, the anniversary is measured less by government statistics than by what she can see and hear beyond her front door.

"It was noticeably enough to where it’s like, ‘Wow, there’s kids actually outside playing,’" she said.

Fox News Digital reached out to Mulroy’s office for comment.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

articles.title: The Fed just threw a wrench in Trump's midterm economic message
articles.excerpt: Gramercy Funds Management Chairman Mohamed El-Erian breaks down Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh's decision to raise interest rates for the first time in three years despite President Donald Trump...
articles.body_text:
Gramercy Funds Management Chairman Mohamed El-Erian breaks down Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh's decision to raise interest rates for the first time in three years despite President Donald Trump's opposition, examining the potential impact on inflation, financial markets, economic growth and what the move could mean for consumers and investors on 'America Reports.'

With the midterms looming, President Donald Trump wants lower interest rates to ease the squeeze on American families. Instead, the Federal Reserve raised rates on Wednesday.

The decision is aimed at combating stubborn inflation, but it will make borrowing more expensive for voters and delivers a big hit to Trump's economic promises with less than two months until Americans cast their ballots and determine which party will control Congress.

The Fed does not set the prices of groceries, cars or homes. But its decisions affect how much Americans pay to borrow money, especially when they buy a house or car. Higher rates can add hundreds of dollars to monthly payments, even when the price of the home or vehicle has not changed.

ONE LITTLE-KNOWN MEETING HELPS DECIDE WHAT AMERICANS CAN AFFORD — AND WHAT THEY CAN’T

The Federal Reserve sets the nation’s interest-rate policy, influencing borrowing costs for households and businesses. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

The Federal Open Market Committee, or FOMC, raised the federal funds rate by a quarter of a percentage point Wednesday, bringing it to a range of 3.75% to 4%. The increase — the Fed’s first in three years — was aimed at slowing inflation, which remains above the central bank’s 2% goal. Higher energy prices and tariffs have added to pressure on household budgets, and the Fed’s projections indicate that another rate increase could come later this year if inflation remains elevated.

The rate hike puts Kevin Warsh, Trump’s pick to lead the world’s most powerful central bank, at odds with the president’s push for lower borrowing costs.

The decision could strain their relationship and revive memories of Trump’s repeated clashes with former Fed Chair Jerome Powell.

TRUMP DANGLES $5,000 CHECKS AS DEBT SURGES — BUT ONLY IF GOP CAN CLEAR MAJOR MIDTERM HURDLE

The rate hike also puts Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh in the spotlight. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images)

Although the president appoints members of the Fed’s Board of Governors, the FOMC is designed to make rate decisions based on economic conditions rather than political pressure.

Warsh underscored that independence Wednesday, saying the Fed acted based on its assessment of employment, the strength of the economy and the inflation outlook.

WARSH FACES FIRST BIG TEST ON CAPITOL HILL AS TRUMP’S FED VISION COMES INTO FOCUS

The Fed chairman was later asked what message he had for Trump, who has repeatedly called for lower rates.

He declined to discuss the president, saying, "I’ve got nothing for you on a discussion with the president."

President Trump nominated Kevin Warsh to lead the Federal Reserve, but Warsh’s rate hike conflicts with the president’s calls for lower borrowing costs. (Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images)

The White House did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

He campaigned on improving affordability, but the rate increase could make it harder for households to feel financial relief—and for the administration to show voters that its economic promises are producing results. With affordability and the cost of living already central issues in the midterm elections, higher borrowing costs could further complicate the president’s economic message.

Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

articles.title: Dem megadonor unleashes reality check on Harris for 2028 while eying socialist firebrand
articles.excerpt: LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman calls another Harris presidential run a ‘very challenging path’ and says potential support for Ocasio-Cortez would depend partly on her opponent and approach to busine...
articles.body_text:
LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman calls another Harris presidential run a ‘very challenging path’ and says potential support for Ocasio-Cortez would depend partly on her opponent and approach to business. (Credit: POLITICO'S Decoded Summit - Sep. 16)

One of Kamala Harris' biggest billionaire backers in 2024 is already casting doubt on another White House bid — while showing surprising openness to a potential 2028 contender from a very different corner of the Democratic Party.

LinkedIn co-founder and Democratic megadonor Reid Hoffman called another Harris presidential run a "very challenging path" Wednesday before leaving the door open to supporting Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and describing the progressive firebrand as "pragmatic."

"It depends a little bit," Hoffman said when asked during POLITICO's Decoded Summit Wednesday in the nation's capital whether he would support Ocasio-Cortez for a 2028 run. "I think she's much more pragmatic than people give her credit for."

The comments mark a notable contrast for Hoffman, who poured millions of dollars into helping elect Harris in 2024 and rallied other Silicon Valley donors behind her campaign after former President Joe Biden ended his re-election bid. Asked Wednesday whether Harris should try again in 2028, Hoffman pointed to what he expects to be a crowded Democratic field.

WATCH: AOC WON'T RULE OUT WHITE HOUSE BID AFTER POLL NAMES HER DEMOCRATS' TOP 2028 PICK

LinkedIn co-founder and Democratic megadonor Reid Hoffman, left, and former Vice President Kamala Harris, right. Hoffman poured millions into supporting Harris' 2024 presidential campaign but questioned her path to another White House bid during remarks Wednesday. (Getty Images)

"I think it would be a very challenging path for her, and it's going to be a very noisy field," Hoffman said in response.

KAMALA HARRIS IS THE 'FAIRLY OBVIOUS' 2028 PRESIDENTIAL FRONTRUNNER, DEMOCRATIC INSIDERS SAY

Hoffman's answer was not an endorsement, however. He said any potential support for Ocasio-Cortez would depend in part on whom she was running against, before Hoffman laid out the qualities he would look for in a candidate.

"If you're basically kind of pro-society, which she is, and pro-business, which is a question, that tends to be where I think the right focal points are," Hoffman said.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. (Drew Angerer/Getty Images)

Meanwhile, two years earlier, Hoffman had made a similar case for Harris, pitching her to hundreds of venture capitalists as "a great centrist" who cared about both society and business, according to a report from the Washington Post.

"She is a great centrist in that she cares about a greater society, and cares about business," Hoffman said during a virtual "VCs for Harris" rally in 2024, according to the Washington Post.

Hoffman’s comments this week about Harris' potential 2028 bid also came days after California Gov. Gavin Newsom said he would not seek the presidency if Harris entered the 2028 race.

Republican strategist Mark Bednar, who previously worked for then-House Speaker Kevin McCarthy, interpreted the two developments as early signs of uncertainty surrounding Harris' position in the emerging Democratic field.

GAVIN NEWSOM SAYS HE WON'T RUN FOR PRESIDENT IN 2028 IF KAMALA HARRIS RUNS

"The idea of pouring cold water over Kamala for others to step forward seems to be very real," Bednar told Fox News Digital. "I don't know if it's directly connected to Newsom in that instance, but it's super interesting how it happens the day after."

Bednar, meanwhile, described Newsom's comments about his potential 2028 presidential run as a "smoke signal to Democratic donors" that "you guys are going to have to be the ones that be the bad cop here because I'm just going to be the good cop in public."

"If you read between the lines, he's signaling to his donors and to his prospective donors, ‘Hey, you guys need to do the dirty work to get her out of the race,’" Bednar said.

Fox News Digital reached out to representatives for Harris, Ocasio-Cortez and Hoffman, but did not receive a response in time for publication.

Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

articles.title: EU announces plan to restrict social media access for under-15s
articles.excerpt:
The EU has announced plans to restrict social media access for under-15s across its member states, in a bid to increase wellbeing and tackle online safety.

Under the plans, there would be a gradual a...
articles.body_text:
The EU has announced plans to restrict social media access for under-15s across its member states, in a bid to increase wellbeing and tackle online safety.

Under the plans, there would be a gradual approach to children using social media which would include banning under 13s from accessing platforms.

Those aged 13 to 15 would only be able to access platforms for an hour per day via "mini accounts" set up through their parent or guardian's social media account.

The European Commission said social media companies would need to prove platforms were safe by design or face fines of up to 6% of their global sales. EU chief Ursula von der Leyen said the move would "put parents back in the driving seat".

She added the legislation - called the EU Kids Act - would give parents "the tools to help their children navigate a safer world".

The restrictions would not just affect well-known apps such as TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat but also YouTube and other video sharing platforms as well as AI chatbots and online games.

"Too many children are being exposed too early to an online world they are not ready to navigate - an environment where bullying can follow you home, where every mistake can be recorded forever," von der Leyen said.

Under the act, only children aged 15 and over would be able to set up their own social media accounts.

But von der Leyen told the EU Parliament on Thursday that "an age limit does not mean letting tech companies off the hook for the content on the platform".

She added that under the legislation - if it is approved - companies would be required to submit detailed child safety plans.

"For every person under 18, the platforms must follow the principal of safety by design, no toxic or addictive features, no traps, etc," she said.

Some individual EU countries have already announced their own separate plans to restrict social media for children, including France and Spain.

Any potential EU-wide legislation would supersede those, but it would be possible for individual EU members to then go further than the bloc's action.

Already there are questions about how this EU-wide legislation would be enforced and the plans are likely to face opposition in the months to come.

France provides an indication of how the path ahead could be bumpy as individual member states may try to strength or weaken the proposals.

The Macron government drew up legislation for a ban on social media for under-15s but last month the country's top court blocked it, ruling that it infringed upon freedom of expression.

French ministers have now amended their original plans.

Some critics of social media bans for children cite privacy concerns.

They worry about teenagers being forced to submit personal information as they go through an age verification process to prove they are old enough to access platforms.

The Commission has said age would be verified using the EU's preexisting age verification app, and no personal data would be collected or shared.

Social media companies will also make their position on the restrictions clear as the act is debated in the months to come.

Von der Leyen had previously proposed a social media "delay" for children in Europe,  saying in May that "the discussion about a minimum age for social media can no longer be ignored".

The policy, formally outlined on Thursday, was also trailed in the EU chief's annual address on Wednesday.

Von der Leyen said there was a "robust body of evidence" on social media harms

In July, the EU said Meta must change the "addictive" design of Facebook and Instagram or face a heavy fine.

In preliminary findings, the European Commission said features such as infinite scroll, autoplaying videos and personalised recommendations could encourage "compulsive use", particularly among children and teens.

A spokesperson for the tech giant told the BBC it disagreed with the findings "which don't accurately take into account the significant steps we've taken to protect teens".

In a separate case, Meta agreed in August to a $18bn (£13.3bn) settlement with US states and territories to resolve claims that Facebook and Instagram harmed children. It denied any wrongdoing as part of the settlement.

The European Commission said its proposed legislation built on findings, external from its special panel on child safety online, which recommended age-appropriate regulation for children, with different guidance for each age group.

It also cited recent EU survey data, external, which found 92% of respondents considered the need to strengthen children's protection online as a top policy priority.

Von der Leyen said the Commission had "looked at Australia" - which banned social media platforms for under-16s last year - when putting together the proposal.

The ban has been difficult for the country to enforce, with its Communications Minister Anika Wells admitting earlier this month that so far no tech firm had been fined despite research showing many under-16s were still on platforms.

A similar ban for under-16s is set to come into force in the UK in spring next year.
