The Anthropic researcher who is leaving the co...
articles.body_text:
Former Anthropic researcher Jason Coxon discusses his resignation from the company and concerns over artificial intelligence safety on ‘Special Report.’

The Anthropic researcher who is leaving the company over fears the technology is gambling with human life told Fox News there is hope that we can avoid the chance it could destroy humankind within the next decade.

Speaking exclusively Wednesday on "Special Report," Jacob Coxon, 27, said regulation is key.

He posted his resignation Tuesday on X, writing that companies are not acting responsibly and that the race toward self-improving superintelligence is "gambling with our lives."

Coxon, who said he spent the past three years doing pretraining research at OpenAI and Anthropic, noted that it's not a completely hopeless scenario.

ANTHROPIC RESEARCHER SAYS AI HAS OVER 10% CHANCE TO 'KILL ALL HUMANS' WITHIN NEXT DECADE

A laptop shows the letters "AI" beside a smartphone displaying a chat AI app logo in Frankfurt, Germany, on Jan. 2, 2025. (Kirill Kudryavtsev/AFP via Getty Images)

He told Fox News chief political anchor Bret Baier the problem is "eminently solvable." He believes there is "definitely" something the country can do to change the dynamic of the "greater than 10% chance" that AI kills all humans.

"It's not like we think this is some impossible thing," Coxon said. "It's just we're racing so fast. We haven't got time to, to solve it correctly. We're not being careful and everyone wants to be careful. I think it's just people are begging for regulation. I think it's just a matter of international somebody stepping in and being able to ensure that we don't race ourselves into extinction. The problem is eminently solvable."

Evan Hubinger, alignment science lead at Anthropic, expressed his agreement with Coxon's X post.

"Jacob is correct here — we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!" he wrote on X. "I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to."

SANDERS PUSHES 'DEATH PENALTY' FOR CRUCIAL US INDUSTRY THAT COULD GIVE ADVANTAGE TO FOREIGN ADVERSARIES

Jacob Coxon is a former Anthropic researcher who left the company over fears the technology could take over the human race. (Thomas Trutschel/Photothek via Getty Images)

"To be clear, as we say in our latest Risk Report, I think the risk from present models is low," Hubinger added. "What I am worried about is superintelligence arising from recursive self-improvement, as we have said is happening faster than we thought."

Coxon said he agrees with Hubinger that right now, the threat is "minimal" of artificial intelligence's actual takeover.

"But recursive self-improvement — this AIs making themselves smarter — could happen as soon as next year," he added. "Some people even say six months. So this attitude is shared across the industry, where people essentially are aware that the work they are currently doing, if we don't slow down, could lead to AI takeover by the end of the decade."

The technology is being used on the international stage as a "superweapon" in an arms race, Coxon said, calling for the global community to provide oversight.

"This is possibly the most dangerous technology that humanity has ever created," he continued. "It's basically out of science fiction. I think we have no other choice but to cooperate internationally because an arms race would be disastrous in a way that no other human activity has been in the past."

Coxon mentioned that a number of technology leaders have publicly expressed the need for a slow-down agreement, but people are not yet taking them seriously.

"It's not just a marketing stunt," he said. "These people are deadly serious that they think their industry needs to be regulated as soon as possible."

As for AI benefit, Coxon said we are "on the doorstep of tremendous discoveries," but we're running in too quickly, calling for moderation.

Baier asked Coxon if the issue could be figured out.

"I think definitely. I think if we actually try instead of submitting to the inevitability of a doomed race or a hubristic gamble, then we can solve it," he said. "The problem is not unsolvable."

Fox News Digital reached out to Anthropic for comment.

Sydney is an editor with Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to sydney.shea@fox.com.

articles.title: US Open winner Andy Roddick defends late finishes amid criticism after Ben Shelton-Carlos Alcaraz thriller
articles.excerpt: Jason Stacy, Aryna Sabalenka's performance coach, joins 'Fox & Friends Weekend' to demonstrate the specialized training drills that keep the tennis star calm under pressure. Stacy explains how mental ...
articles.body_text:
Jason Stacy, Aryna Sabalenka's performance coach, joins 'Fox & Friends Weekend' to demonstrate the specialized training drills that keep the tennis star calm under pressure. Stacy explains how mental strength training helps Sabalenka manage her emotions during high-stakes matches. The hosts participate in a live demonstration of these reaction and coordination drills in the studio.

Retired American tennis star Andy Roddick weighed in on Ben Shelton’s five-set victory over Carlos Alcaraz at the U.S. Open, which ended in the early hours of Wednesday morning.

Shelton secured the biggest victory of his young professional career in a tiebreaker shortly after 3:30 a.m. ET, becoming the first American man to defeat either Alcaraz or Jannik Sinner at a Grand Slam. His victory, coupled with Frances Tiafoe’s five-set win over fellow American Alex Michelsen in the other men’s quarterfinal, guaranteed that at least one American would reach the 2026 U.S. Open final.

The last time an American-born man brought home the men's singles title at the U.S. Open was in 2003, when Roddick won his lone Grand Slam.

Ben Shelton of the United States (R) shakes hands with Spain's Carlos Alcaraz after winning the men's singles quarter-final tennis match on day ten of the U.S. Open tennis tournament at the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center in New York City on Sept. 9, 2026. (Leonardo MUNOZ / AFP via Getty Images)

On a recent edition of his "Served" podcast, Roddick addressed criticism surrounding the tournament's late-night schedule and overall logistics, making clear he had no regrets about how the match ultimately turned out.

NOVAK DJOKOVIC SUFFERS STUNNING DEFEAT IN FIRST ROUND OF US OPEN AFTER TRYING TO BATTLE THROUGH AILMENTS

"I know a lot of the comments are, you know, ‘How do you finish at four in the morning?’ and all of that," Roddick said. "Well, every match goes to a match tiebreak except for one. And you’ve got to get 25,000 people out of a stadium responsibly, and you’ve got to get 25,000 people in responsibly. So, I hear a lot of complaining. I don’t hear a lot of proposed solutions."

Andy Roddick looks on during an exhibition doubles match against Switzerland’s Roger Federer and John McEnroe at the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center during Fan Week on Aug. 25, 2026, in Flushing, Queens, New York City. (Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images)

Roddick stood by the Grand Slam's late-night session format while conceding that a five-hour match could test viewers’ patience, echoing a concern raised by sports podcaster Bill Simmons.

"Starting earlier wasn’t possible because of Frances and Mickelson’s match," Roddick said. "And so, you have to have a night session at the US Open. It’s one of the things that we all love. And they’ve been on the wrong side of luck. Now, I know there are some people who have said shorter format. And I know Bill Simmons made the point that this is ridiculous, that we’re playing too long. He’s normally well-thought-out in his thoughts. I don’t disagree with the premise that, like, ‘Five hours is too much. I’m bored.'"

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"7-6 in the fifth last night for Ben Shelton and Carlos Alcaraz in that match, where Tiafoe is down two sets, and the guy’s serving for it — I kind of like the fact that we have a sport where you get into these long-form matches, and it’s the hardest thing on earth," Roddick said. "It’s the hardest sport in the world. If you take that away, can we lay that claim anymore? I don’t know."

Ben Shelton of the United States is congratulated by Carlos Alcaraz of Spain after winning their quarterfinal match at the U.S. Open tennis championships on Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo/Adam Hunger)

Roddick acknowledged the practical case for a shorter format, noting the challenges a late-night match can pose for those working behind the scenes.

"I understand all the pragmatists out there that say we should have a shorter format. I understand the reasons for it. I understand that it’s inconvenient for Sean to be up until 4:00 a.m., you know, watching this match while he’s editing last night’s show," Roddick said. "I understand that some people have to go to sleep because, like you, I had to go to sleep to protect my workday today. I understand all of the rational arguments."

On Friday, Tiafoe and Shelton will meet on center court at Arthur Ashe Stadium, named for the 1968 champion who remains the last Black American man to win the U.S. Open men’s singles title.

Chantz Martin is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Deadly Philippines ferry fire leaves scores of people missing
articles.excerpt:
Forty-three people rescued and early death toll stands at five after blaze aboard MV ‌June Aster in waters off Coron, Palawan, says coast guard

Five people were confirmed dead ⁠in early counting and ...
articles.body_text:
Forty-three people rescued and early death toll stands at five after blaze aboard MV ‌June Aster in waters off Coron, Palawan, says coast guard

Five people were confirmed dead ⁠in early counting and ​more than 80 were missing after a ferry caught fire ⁠off Palawan island in the western Philippines on Wednesday night, the Philippine coast ⁠guard said.

Forty-three people were ​rescued from the MV ‌June Aster in waters off Coron, Palawan, the coast guard said. Footage showed flames engulfing parts of the vessel and responders placing victims ‌in body bags.

Coast guard spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab told DZXL radio the vessel’s manifest listed 117 passengers and 17 crew members.

Based on the reported number of survivors and fatalities, more than ⁠80 people were unaccounted for, and Cayabyab ​said ​the figures might change ​as the rescue operation continued.

The ​ferry had ‌departed from ​Baseco ​in Manila and was bound for Coron, she said.

The cause of the fire was under investigation.

articles.title: Talarico says he 'missed the mark' as he backtracks on controversial woke statements
articles.excerpt:
Democrat James Talarico reversed several of his most controversial takes as a critical Senate race tightens in Texas.

In a Fox News exclusive interview, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico cam...
articles.body_text:
Democrat James Talarico reversed several of his most controversial takes as a critical Senate race tightens in Texas.

In a Fox News exclusive interview, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico came out in favor of banning gender surgery for minors and opposed transgender-identifying men competing in women’s sports.

Talarico also backtracked on several of his more controversial claims, including saying there are six genders and that "God is nonbinary."

This comes as the Texas Senate race, which is surprisingly close according to recent Fox News polling, enters its final months. The race is considered critical to both parties' chances of securing a Senate majority. Talarico is facing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican who has faced controversies of his own. A Republican loss in Texas would significantly impact President Donald Trump's ability to implement his agenda.

Fox News spoke with Talarico at a food drive campaign event in Dallas on Tuesday. Talarico’s event took place as the first-ever GOP midterm convention kicked off just miles away in downtown Dallas.

TALARICO CAMPAIGNS WITH SURGEON WHO OPERATED ON TRANSGENDER MINORS: ‘WOLF IN SHEEP’S CLOTHING’

Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico speaks during a campaign rally at the Cailloux Theater on Aug. 31, 2026, in Kerrville, Texas. Talarico is campaigning across the state in a close race against Republican candidate and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton ahead of the Nov. 3 general election. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

Asked whether he would vote as a U.S. senator in favor of a national ban on gender surgery for minors, Talarico answered, "Absolutely."

He said, "I've been consistent on this issue," explaining his opposition to a Texas bill to ban transgender surgeries on minors by saying the measure "was overly broad."

"If you go back and check, I voted for a major amendment to limit the bill to banning surgeries for minors," he said. "As a lawmaker, my job is to try to sift through everything the bill does. And sometimes there's stuff in it that's really harmful, and I have no choice but to oppose the bill as a whole."

"It's why I try to use amendments, to narrow the focus of the bill so that it does exactly what we intend it to do," he continued. "It's what I tried to do with that piece of legislation, and unfortunately the amendment I supported was unsuccessful."

In 2023, as a member of the Texas House of Representatives, Talarico voted against a state bill titled SB 14, which prohibited certain gender surgery, puberty blockers and certain hormone treatments for minors. There were 18 amendments to the bill proposed by Democrats, all of which Talarico voted in favor and all of which ultimately failed.

In the same interview, Talarico acknowledged that men in women’s sports is a significant issue in Texas. He said, "I oppose trans athletes playing in girls’ sports if it endangers safety or fairness."

"Every sport has to be safe and fair. As a former public school teacher, I care a lot about our student athletes. I care a lot about our students. And so, I will oppose trans athletes playing in girls’ sports if it risks safety or fairness," he said.

JAMES TALARICO ADMITS PAST COMMENTS 'MISSED THE MARK' WHEN CONFRONTED ON CLAIMS LIKE GOD IS 'NON-BINARY'

Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico speaks to volunteers at a "Love Thy Neighbor" Statewide Grocery Drive on September 09, 2026 in Dallas, Texas. Talarico continues campaigning across the state in a close race with Republican candidate, state Attorney General Ken Paxton ahead of the November 3 general elections. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

He also addressed perhaps his most controversial statement, which he made in 2021, while opposing a Texas bill to keep men out of women’s sports. Talarico said on the state House floor that "God is both masculine and feminine and everything in between. God is non-binary."

"I was being provocative with that statement. I get that," Talarico admitted, explaining, "What I was trying to say is that you can't use human categories to define God, and that's not controversial theologically."

Regarding his past comment about there being more than two genders, Talarico said he does not currently believe there are six sexes.

"I've missed the mark on some of my past statements. I will be the first to admit it," he said. "What I meant is that there are two sexes, and then there's a small percentage of people with genetic abnormalities."

"Obviously didn't say it correctly. There are not six sexes. There are two, and I think the reason that politicians in that convention center across the street want to talk about six sexes is because they don't want to talk about $6 diesel," he said.

Though he walked back these controversies, Talarico did not hold back on his criticism of the Supreme Court, which he described as "infected" with corruption, saying it "needs to be overhauled."

LONGTIME GOP AIDE DEFECTS TO DEM RISING STAR AS TEXAS SENATE BATTLE FOR CORNYN'S SEAT HEATS UP

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton is urging the Republican Party to start spending now in the ballyhooed Senate race in the largest red state. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

He said that if elected, "You're going to expect that I will vote for overhaul to the Supreme Court. That will include binding codes of conduct for our justices. It'll include term limits, and I am open to a discussion about expanding the number of justices."

Following these controversies, Talarico pledged to keep his message focused on affordability for the remainder of the campaign.

"Everywhere I go across the state of Texas, people are struggling to survive in this economy. They are struggling to afford the basics: groceries, gas, utilities, healthcare. And that's what I'm going to be focused on from now until Election Day."

On the topic of affordability, Talarico said that "we should not have a state income tax" in Texas. This is despite Talarico previously voting against a measure to permanently ban a state income tax, which he suggested was redundant and an example of "government waste at its worst." The measure was ultimately passed by the Texas Legislature and approved by Texas voters in November 2019.

He knocked Paxton as "the most corrupt politician in Texas," saying, "He's going to try to clip some of my comments, including comments where I was being a little provocative in order to try to distract from that career."

Fox News Digital reached out to the Paxton campaign for a response.

Brooke Taylor is a Dallas-based correspondent for FOX News Channel (FNC). She joined the network in 2024.

articles.title: George W Bush recalls moment with Derek Jeter before nerve-wracking pitch at Yankee Stadium after 9/11
articles.excerpt: O'Hara's Restaurant and Pub serves as a historic sanctuary for first responders near Ground Zero. Steve Doocy reports live from the venue alongside former NYPD Chief of Department John Chell to reflec...
articles.body_text:
O'Hara's Restaurant and Pub serves as a historic sanctuary for first responders near Ground Zero. Steve Doocy reports live from the venue alongside former NYPD Chief of Department John Chell to reflect on the legacy of 9/11.

Former President George W. Bush recalled Wednesday a lighthearted moment he shared with New York Yankees shortstop Derek Jeter before throwing out a ceremonial first pitch at Yankee Stadium just weeks after 9/11.

Bush told the story alongside Condoleezza Rice, his national security advisor at the time of the attacks, during a reunification event at the George W. Bush Presidential Center in Dallas, Texas.

During the World Series in October 2001, Bush said he was feeling the pressure of leading the nation through a fragile moment when Jeter told him before the game, "Don’t bounce it, they’ll boo you."

As the audience chuckled at the joke, Bush recalled feeling the raw emotions inside the NYC stadium as he walked to the mound at center field.

GEORGE BUSH WELCOMES TOP OFFICIALS TO HIS HOME STATE FOR 9/11 REMEMBRANCE ON 25TH ANNIVERSARY OF ATTACKS

Former President George W. Bush speaks during a 9/11 remembrance event at the George W. Bush Presidential Center in Dallas, Texas. (Pool)

"I looked at the catcher, he looked really tiny, and the ball felt really heavy," Bush said.

While scanning the faces in the crowd, Bush said he could imagine people thinking, "You can knock down our buildings, but you d— sure not going to touch our soul."

AMERICA’S HEARTLAND COMES FACE-TO-FACE WITH 9/11 HISTORY AS 25TH ANNIVERSARY NEARS

President George W. Bush throws the ceremonial first pitch prior to Game Three of the 2001 World Series between the Arizona Diamondbacks and the New York Yankees at Yankee Stadium on Oct. 30, 2001 in Bronx, New York.  (Rich Pilling/MLB via Getty Images)

Bush recalled throwing the ball, which made it over the plate, and described the moment as "memorable."

"I mean, it was an amazing feeling," he said.

NEW YORK, NY - SEPTEMBER 2001: A view of the World Trade Center rubble is seen in this file photo from early September 2001 shortly after the 9/11 terrorist attacks in New York City. (Jane Tyska / Digital First Media / East Bay Times via Getty Images)

This coming Friday will mark the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, when al-Qaeda terrorists hijacked four commercial airplanes in a coordinated attack against the United States.

Two of the flights struck New York City’s Twin Towers at the World Trade Center, sending both buildings crashing down and causing mass casualties. A third flight struck the Pentagon in Washington, D.C., while the fourth crashed in a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania.

Nearly 3,000 people died in the terror attacks, including hundreds of firefighters and police officers.

Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

articles.title: Instagram boss says users will be ‘overwhelmed’ with brand content in algorithm-free world
articles.excerpt:
Adam Mosseri says platform’s algorithm ‘feels like a black box’ but company trying to give users more control after Labor announces opt-out plan

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates...
articles.body_text:
Adam Mosseri says platform’s algorithm ‘feels like a black box’ but company trying to give users more control after Labor announces opt-out plan

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

Instagram’s chief executive has said users will have a worse experience in an algorithm-free world, seeing more brand-related content, and spend less time on the app.

The comments come as the Australian government plans to give users the option to opt out of algorithms, with the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, announcing plans on Tuesday to require social media platforms to prompt users to choose between a feed of algorithm-recommended content or a reverse chronological feed of the pages users follow. Labor also plans to introduce a range of measures designed to address online harm on the sites.

In a briefing with journalists on Thursday to launch the company’s Algo Confessions series in Australia, Instagram’s chief executive, Adam Mosseri, did not comment directly on the Albanese government proposal but said Instagram had a range of algorithms in operation. Those include ranking which friends’ stories you see more often, or which users come up first in message suggestions based on interactions, as well as the algorithm that determines the content people see in their feeds.

The launch of the series in Australia is the first outside the US. It features celebrities and influencers detailing how Instagram determines what content ends up in a user’s feed, and how the user can have some control over that by adding or removing tags in their settings.

Mosseri said just a “very vocal minority” wants social media to go back to reverse chronological feeds, which he said would just incentivise people to post more.

“What ends up happening is the best way to get more reach is just to post more often and those who can afford to post the most often do and then therefore get the most reach,” he said.

“And it turns out your friends post a lot less than creators, who post a lot less than brands and companies.”

He said people would be “overwhelmed” with content from brands, and creators and friends would be drowned out.

“What happens is people become a bit less interested in the experience and they use it a lot less, which then means that there’s less reach to go around and people start to get more and more mad about the fact that their reach is going down because the overall pie gets smaller.”

He said engagement and user satisfaction goes down.

“It’s this interesting tension between what an individual might want and what happens when you actually explode that to the entire community,” he said.

“That’s not to say that ranking is perfect, it’s not, we make mistakes – one of the things that frustrates me about ranking is that we end up over-optimising for things that we can measure and undervaluing things that are more difficult to measure.”

Mosseri said Instagram’s ranking algorithm “feels like a black box” but was something Instagram was trying to give users more control over by opting out of certain topics in their recommendations.

He said in the future, Meta’s AI models could eventually allow users to talk to the app to understand why they are seeing certain types of content.

Mosseri said he did not believe the app to be the clinical definition of “addictive”.

“I don’t believe Instagram is addictive – I know that is controversial to say – I do think we often in English anyway conflate the way we colloquially use the word addicted … like ‘I’m addicted to this show and I’m binge watching it, which is not good for me’.”

He said clinically defined addictions have withdrawal symptoms, while social media does not have that effect, and “those things are different”.

Mosseri has made this claim before. Research has found some users can have an impulse to use a platform without being fully aware of it, and evidence shows frequent engagement with algorithms “alters dopamine pathways” that fosters dependency that is “analogous to substance addiction”.

In the landmark US court case centred on the addictive nature of Meta’s products, the company’s lawyer last month conceded to the court that it was “no dispute” people can struggle with social media, but the company has tools to address that. Meta later settled the case for US$18bn while denying any wrongdoing.

articles.title: SMH columnist Peter FitzSimons tells Alan Jones trial alleged victim was ‘revolted’ by abuse
articles.excerpt:
FitzSimons tells court that complainant C told him Jones, who has pleaded not guilty, would touch his penis and he ‘kept pushing it away’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get o...
articles.body_text:
FitzSimons tells court that complainant C told him Jones, who has pleaded not guilty, would touch his penis and he ‘kept pushing it away’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Sydney Morning Herald columnist Peter FitzSimons has told the Alan Jones trial an alleged victim he spoke to in 2019 was “tearful” and sounded “emotionally traumatised” when detailing alleged assaults by the 2GB broadcaster.

The commentator and author gave evidence in the Downing Centre local court on Thursday about a telephone call he had with the alleged victim known as complainant C in October 2019.

He said the man, who remained anonymous to FitzSimons, alleged that Jones, a decade earlier, had pushed him against the wall of a lift and kissed him “romantically” at the broadcaster’s Circular Quay apartment.

C also described a Christmas lunch where Jones was “gripping his penis” under the table, FitzSimons told the court on Thursday.

“He was very tearful … he was very, very upset,” FitzSimons told the Sydney court. “It was clear I was speaking to someone who was emotionally traumatised.”

The journalist said the young man told him that Jones would touch his leg and his penis while he was driving for him.

“He said I didn’t say no … but I kept pushing it away,” FitzSimons said.

Jones has pleaded not guilty to 20 charges of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching in relation to six men. Eight of the charges relate to complainant C.

FitzSimons said he was put in contact with C by 2GB broadcaster Ray Hadley and he took notes of the conversation on his computer, later sharing them with SMH investigative reporter Kate McClymont.

Hadley has previously told the court the conversation lasted between 30 and 40 minutes.

“He made it clear he was revolted by what happened but he was deeply upset for not being stronger,” FitzSimons said of his phone conversation with C.

FitzSimons said C explained that he was a junior employee at 2GB and in his early 20s and Jones was “the sun king” when he started paying attention to him and complimenting him. Jones eventually offered him a job as a driver.

The court heard C told FitzSimons he was “thrilled to be driving for Jones” and he couldn’t believe the “No 1 person” at 2GB was noticing him.

FitzSimons said C told him that in between the compliments Jones would occasionally give him a “blast”.

After a period of time, Jones began to touch him inappropriately, including at a lunch when he was sitting next to the broadcaster, C said, according to the SMH columnist.

“He said that while he was sitting next to Mr Jones, Mr Jones’s hand went on to his penis and he was gripping his penis,” FitzSimons said on Thursday. “It was under the table.”

The witness said C told him that two men were “laughing at his discomfort” and one of those two senior media identities was 2GB broadcaster Jason Morrison.

FitzSimons said Hadley later told him that C was emotionally fragile and was “spiralling” and he agreed not to pursue a story.

The columnist was later cross-examined by Jones’s barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC.

The court heard that FitzSimons’ contemporaneous notes said C alleged Jones would put his hand on his thigh and then “manipulate my penis”.

Bashir questioned FitzSimons about why he said thigh in one account and knee during his evidence in chief.

“You will appreciate the difference between the knee and the thigh is a matter of two inches,” FitzSimons replied.

He agreed with Bashir that he had a “long-standing and publicly recorded” dislike of Jones and that before his conversation with C he had written in the Herald: “Alan Jones is a malignant tumour on the body politic of this city, this state and this country and the sooner he is excised the better.”

FitzSimons said in court he did not resile from writing the words. “I am very proud of that line,” he said.

FitzSimons agreed he had written that he wanted Jones to retire and “stop bullying 10 people a day” and stop “giving a platform to the execrable Pauline Hanson”.

He told the court he stood by those comments. The trial before judge Glenn Walsh continues.

articles.title: Rhode Island’s Democratic governor loses primary amid anger over bridge
articles.excerpt:
Helena Foulkes beats incumbent Dan McKee after criticizing handling of Providence’s Washington bridge, now expected to be completed in 2028

Rhode Island’s Dan McKee became the first sitting governor ...
articles.body_text:
Helena Foulkes beats incumbent Dan McKee after criticizing handling of Providence’s Washington bridge, now expected to be completed in 2028

Rhode Island’s Dan McKee became the first sitting governor to lose a primary in nearly a decade, bested not by a more progressive challenger or a more youthful upset but by frustration over a bridge.

McKee lost his Democratic primary to Helena Foulkes, a former longtime executive with Rhode Island-based retail pharmacy CVS, the Associated Press said on Wednesday.

“Tonight, we may have won the Democratic primary for governor, but let me be clear about what happens next: you will have a governor for everyone,” Foulkes said during her victory speech in the state’s capital, Providence. “Because there is so much work that needs to be done, and we need to do this together.”

It is rare for a sitting governor to lose a primary election. It hasn’t happened in Rhode Island since 1994.

In his concession speech, also in Providence, McKee promised to work with Foulkes to ensure she is elected in November.

“This is something that I think is difficult to deal with,” McKee said, “but we just got to hold our heads high.”

Several Democratic incumbents have been toppled this cycle, in a wave of anti-establishment anger that has elevated young and progressive insurgents. But this contest was different.

On the campaign trail, Foulkes criticized McKee’s handling of repair work on Providence’s Washington bridge, a major east-west traffic artery that carries roughly 100,000 vehicles per day. She accused him of bungling those repairs, which have dragged on longer than originally planned.

McKee closed the bridge in December 2023, after inspectors uncovered serious structural problems. By March 2024, officials had concluded that repairing the structure was not feasible and that it would have to be rebuilt. State officials initially estimated that the bridge would be reopened to traffic this year, but the project’s completion date has since been delayed to November 2028.

The primary contest was something of a rematch from four years ago, when Foulkes, who is the niece of former Democratic Senator Chris Dodd of Connecticut, came in a close second behind McKee in a five-way contest. McKee went on to easily win the general election in 2022, after having assumed the role from then-governor Gina Raimondo, who stepped down to become Joe Biden’s US commerce secretary in 2021.

Election prognosticators rate the seat as strongly Democratic, and therefore the winner of Wednesday’s primary is seen as having a major advantage in the November general election.

Mckee’s defeat was not the only electoral upset on Wednesday. In Providence, David Morales, a 27-year-old Democratic socialist defeated mayor Brett Smiley in the Democratic primary, ending the incumbent’s bid for a second term. Morales’s campaign was backed by progressive stalwarts, including senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and several labor unions.

articles.title: US forces obliterate suspected 'narco-terrorist' vessel in lethal Eastern Pacific strike, killing 3
articles.excerpt: SOUTHCOM carried out a lethal strike on a go-fast boat along a known trafficking route. Chief Gen. Francis L. Donovan says Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere will "hunt, disrupt, and defeat" cartel n...
articles.body_text:
SOUTHCOM carried out a lethal strike on a go-fast boat along a known trafficking route. Chief Gen. Francis L. Donovan says Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere will "hunt, disrupt, and defeat" cartel networks.

A suspected drug-smuggling vessel was wiped out in a lethal U.S. military strike Wednesday in the Eastern Pacific, killing three alleged "narco-terrorists" aboard, according to the Department of War.

Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere carried out the Sept. 9 strike under the direction of U.S. Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) after intelligence allegedly tied the vessel to drug trafficking.

"Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narco-trafficking," the department said in a post on X. "The operation killed three narco-terrorists."

WHITE HOUSE HIGHLIGHTS 'STEEPEST' EVER DECLINE IN US CASUALTIES FROM CARTELS AMID BOAT STRIKES

The operation marked the latest U.S. attack on suspected cartel vessels accused of moving deadly narcotics along known trafficking routes off the coast of Latin America.

It came less than two weeks after the Pentagon released newly unclassified images to Fox News Digital showing suspected drug boats speeding across open water, including one vessel loaded with what appeared to be bundles of narcotics.

The images, dated Oct. 27, Oct. 29 and Dec. 4, 2025, offered a rare look at suspected smugglers under U.S. military surveillance as the Trump administration intensified its campaign against cartel networks.

EXCLUSIVE: FENTANYL DEATHS PLUNGE 22% AS TRUMP WHITE HOUSE TOUTS CRACKDOWN ON DEADLY DRUG CRISIS

An unclassified Pentagon image dated Oct. 29, 2025, shows a suspected drug-smuggling boat at sea. (Department of War)

An unclassified Pentagon image dated Oct. 27, 2025, shows a suspected drug-smuggling vessel carrying apparent packages at sea. (Department of War)

An unclassified Pentagon image dated Dec. 4, 2025, shows a suspected drug-smuggling vessel carrying apparent packages at sea. (Department of War)

Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson accompanied the release with a deadly warning for traffickers who threaten American communities.

"Nearly one year after the first strike, the message to narco-terrorists remains unchanged: if you traffic deadly illicit narcotics and threaten the American people, we will hunt you down, we will find you, and we will kill you," Wilson told Fox News Digital at the time.

The Pentagon said Operation Southern Spear had carried out 67 strikes as of late August, beginning with the first operation on Sept. 2, 2025.

US MILITARY BOARDS, SEARCHES AND SINKS VESSEL ALLEGEDLY SUPPORTING LOS CHONEROS NARCO-TERRORISTS

The Pentagon said Operation Southern Spear had carried out 67 strikes as of late August. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo, File)

Wilson said the campaign had disrupted trafficking networks, forced smugglers to change their tactics and removed "dangerous narcoterrorists."

"Operation Southern Spear has disrupted trafficking networks, forced trafficker adaptations, removed dangerous narcoterrorists, and demonstrated that the United States will use every lawful tool available to defend our Homeland and protect our communities," Wilson said.

One of the most recent strikes came Aug. 25, when U.S. Southern Command said four alleged drug smugglers were killed aboard a fast boat operating along known trafficking routes in the Caribbean.

"Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel’s active involvement in narco-trafficking," SOUTHCOM said at the time.

US FORCES SINK NARCO-REFUELING STATION LINKED TO ECUADORIAN CARTEL IN PACIFIC: SOUTHCOM

The operation was carried out by Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere under the direction of Gen. Francis L. Donovan.

"Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere continues executing precise, lethal operations against the cartels," Donovan said. "We will hunt, disrupt, and defeat these narco-terrorist networks."

"SOUTHCOM is resolved to neutralizing cartel terror and violence throughout the region and into the U.S. homeland," he added.

Days before that Caribbean strike, the U.S. military said two people were killed in an attack on a vessel in the Eastern Pacific. It was the first reported strike in more than two months.

US MILITARY KILLS THREE 'NARCO-TERRORISTS' IN LATEST LETHAL STRIKE ON VESSEL IN THE EASTERN PACIFIC

Department of War Secretary Pete Hegseth speaks during a news briefing at the Pentagon in Washington, D.C. (Oliver Contreras / AFP via Getty Images, File)

President Donald Trump has described the fight as an "armed conflict" with cartels in Latin America and argued the attacks are necessary to stop drugs from reaching American communities and fueling fatal overdoses.

The administration is also pursuing agreements with allied nations that could extend the campaign onto land in several Latin American countries.

War Secretary Pete Hegseth said during an August visit to Panama that Colombia, Guatemala and Honduras had agreed to allow the U.S. to conduct joint operations against criminal groups on their soil, though Guatemala denied that an agreement had been reached. Ecuador began similar missions with the U.S. in March.

Fox News Digital's Eric Mack contributed to this report.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

articles.title: NDIS data may have ended up in Palantir’s analytics platform as part of efforts to curb fraud
articles.excerpt:
Exclusive: The Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission, which has access to NDIA data, used Palantir as part of a multi-agency fraud taskforce

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news ...
articles.body_text:
Exclusive: The Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission, which has access to NDIA data, used Palantir as part of a multi-agency fraud taskforce

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Personal information of national disability insurance scheme participants may have ended up in controversial software company Palantir’s analytics platform as part of a massive multi-agency sharing program investigating fraud, Guardian Australia can reveal.

There have been calls to ban the use of Palantir’s software by the Australian government since May, after it implied some cultures are inferior to others in a manifesto described by one UK MP as the “ramblings of a supervillain”.

Last month, the national disability insurance agency (NDIA) denied using Palantir’s software, following questions from Guardian Australia after a freedom of information request revealed the agency had met with representatives of the company co-founded by US Trump-aligned billionaire Peter Thiel in 2023.

However, Guardian Australia can reveal data from the agency is being shared with the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission (ACIC) which has used Palantir as part of the Fraud Fusion Taskforce of 25 government agencies that is responsible for investigating fraud.

The taskforce – established in 2022 – is led by the NDIA and Services Australia, while the ACIC is responsible for the Fraud Fusion Centre, which brings in “large volumes of information, data and intelligence” held by agencies that could be relevant to the taskforce’s work, according to documents released under freedom of information.

The ACIC last year said the agency was using “a range of specialist tools … to gather intelligence, advanced data analysis” to “identify behavioural patterns and financial activity, and access to extensive intelligence databases that provide deep insights into serious and organised crime networks”.

ACIC has paid millions in contracts to Palantir in the past few years for its software to map connections between people, and the FoI docs suggest ACIC’s capabilities include bulk data analytics and data-matching across participating agencies’ databases.

Gabrielle Josling, a data scientist and researcher, who filed a number of the freedom of information requests to participating agencies in the taskforce, attempted to obtain from the ACIC records of data from the fraud taskforce or centre being fed into Palantir’s software.

In correspondence from late August, an FoI officer revealed reluctance to process the request given “the process for ingesting one FFC dataset into Palantir generates an amount of documents that … would likely not be manageable.”

A spokesperson for the NDIA confirmed it was sharing participant information with the taskforce.

“NDIS participant information is only shared with Fraud Fusion Taskforce partners on a restricted basis where potential criminal conduct is suspected to protect participants from fraud,” a spokesperson said.

A spokesperson for the ACIC said it used “a suite of analytical tools and capabilities” and taskforce-related data collected and stored by the ACIC is consistent with the restrictions agreed with the provisioning agency.

“The contributing agency is responsible for articulating any use, handling, and disclosure restrictions to the ACIC.”

Tom Sulston, head of policy at Digital Rights Watch said it was “very concerning” if Palantir was being used in the assessment of potential fraud in the NDIS and similar programs.

“People using NDIS deserve the dignity of not being treated like criminals simply for accessing the services that they need to live a full life,” he said.

“The creation of such enormous aggregated datasets is a fundamentally de-humanising application of surveillance technology. That’s particularly awful when targeted at people living with disabilities, who are already regularly subjected to regular dehumanisation and indignities.”

The Greens senator and digital rights and AI spokesperson, David Shoebridge, said the FoI response revealed that “having Palantir inside any one government agency sees millions of data points ingested by this global surveillance vampire”.

“NDIS participants give their data to the agency believing it will be protected and only used to assist in their claims, having it funnelled into Palantir under the guise of fraud prevention is a deep betrayal.”

A spokesperson for Palantir said the company “builds software that helps organisations use their data to make better decisions and solve their most complex problems.

“We are committed to supporting Australian government agencies in tackling complex challenges, including serious financial crime and fraud.”

The supermarket giant Coles announced last week it would not extend its contract with Palantir beyond 2027. Coles had used Palantir software in rostering, store operations and supply chain planning.

articles.title: US slaps import ban on Canadian alcohol and other goods
articles.excerpt:
The US is banning a slew of Canadian products, including alcoholic spirits, dairy goods and motor vehicles, as Canadian retaliatory tariffs on American goods come into force.

In a series of executive...
articles.body_text:
The US is banning a slew of Canadian products, including alcoholic spirits, dairy goods and motor vehicles, as Canadian retaliatory tariffs on American goods come into force.

In a series of executive orders on Tuesday, US President Donald Trump said that Canada is "discriminating" against the United States and outlined the import ban, to begin 29 September.

Earlier on Tuesday, Canada Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a video address that  his country's pivot away from the US as its largest trading partner "will come at a cost".

Both US and Canadian officials have said they would like to strike a trade deal, but no new talks have been scheduled since negotiations collapsed in late August.

The BBC has contacted the office of the Prime Minister of Canada, Mark Carney, for comment.

The White House's new sanctions are the latest strike in a months-long trade war between the US and Canada. The sides have historically been close allies, with each a key business partner to the other.

The US is Canada's largest trading partner - generally more than two-thirds of its total exports go to its neighbour.

On the other hand, Canada is the US' second-largest trading partner, after Mexico, although its exports are far more diversified.

Business owners on both sides of the border have expressed fears over the trade war's fallout. Many expect prices of goods to rise and the number of customers to fall.

Last month, the White House had imposed 50% tariffs on around $20bn (£14.8bn) of Canadian goods after several rounds of talks had broken down.

Those tariffs hit sectors including Canada's furniture and wine industries, as well as sporting and fishing equipment businesses.

Canada responded with dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs on US goods like steel, clothing and furniture. The counter-duties came into effect after midnight on Tuesday.

Canada is "discriminating" against US businesses by restricting the distribution of US goods while not doing the same to such products from other countries, the White House said when announcing the new import restrictions on Tuesday.

The response targets various alcoholic drinks and dairy products like whey, according to a series of White House statements signed by the president.

On Monday, Trump hinted at more trade restrictions to come, warning Canadian aircraft company Bombardier that it would no longer be able to sell its products in the US unless it moves manufacturing there.

Trump has long believed that tariffs will help reduce trade imbalances between the US and other countries, but his wide-ranging tariffs scheme has upset many of the States' traditional allies.

Tension between the US and Canada have now also expanded beyond tariffs.

In August, Trump ordered Lake Ontario to be renamed as Lake America, resulting in uproar from Canadians and some Americans.

What tariffs will really cost Canadians and Americans

articles.body_text:
New Hampshire primary Senate candidates face a key test as attorney Katie Zacharia analyzes the race on 'Fox & Friends First.' Progressive Karishma Manzur challenges Chris Pappas for the Democratic nomination.

Rep. Maggie Goodlander, D-N.H., won her primary to advance to a general election showdown in a Democrat-leaning seat comprising generally the western half of New Hampshire from Massachusetts to the Canadian border.

Goodlander is the wife of former Biden National Security Adviser Jacob Sullivan, and won her first race for the seat in 2024 – succeeding the retiring Rep. Ann Kuster, D-N.H.

While Republicans have dominated the governor’s office in New Hampshire in recent years, Democrats have been largely successful at the congressional level.

The district has been in Democratic hands since 2013 and, prior to that, largely held by Rep. Charles Bass, R-N.H., who served two lengthy tenures interrupted by a Democrat in the mid-1990s.

TRUMP SAYS US MAY RECOVER ALL THE EQUIPMENT LEFT BEHIND IN AFGHANISTAN BY BIDEN ADMIN

Now-Rep. Maggie Goodlander (D-NH) speaks at a campaign event ahead of then-President Joe Biden, at the New Hampshire Democratic Party headquarters, on Oct. 22, 2024 in Concord, N.H. (Fox News - Paul Steinhauser)

Goodlander faced New Hampshire State Rep. Paige Beauchemin, D-Hillsborough, and there is also an independent running in the general election. The winner of a four-way Republican primary Tuesday night was Goodlander’s last opponent, Lily Tang Williams.

Goodlander’s husband’s role in the White House was prominent, as Sullivan was front-and-center during the disastrous Afghanistan withdrawal in 2021, had a role in foreign relations during the early part of the Russia-Ukraine War and helped manage the U.S. relationship with China.

ONE OF CONGRESS' MOST POWERFUL DEMOCRATS JUST SURVIVED A PROGRESSIVE PRIMARY REVOLT

Jake US National Security Adviser Jake Sullivan (C) looks on as US President Joe Biden (R) meets with Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi (L), and Japanese Prime Minister Fumio Kishida during the Quadrilateral Summit at the Archmere Academy in Wilmington, Delaware, on September 21, 2024. (Photo by Brendan SMIALOWSKI / AFP) (Photo by BRENDAN SMIALOWSKI/AFP via Getty Images)

Beauchemin ran against Goodlander from the left, arguing the incumbent has not been sufficiently progressive or effective during her first term.

The district is the more rural of the two, and includes cities like Pittsburg in the forests of northern New Hampshire.

With neighboring Rep. Chris Pappas, D-N.H., giving up his House seat to run for the Senate seat being vacated by Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., the political landscape in the Granite State will look much different no matter what come January.

Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

articles.title: Mamdani releases 170,000 pages of records regarding impact on air quality of the 9/11 attacks
articles.excerpt:
The documents are available through an online portal that was launched three days before the 25th anniversary of September 11

New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration has released more tha...
articles.body_text:
The documents are available through an online portal that was launched three days before the 25th anniversary of September 11

New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration has released more than 170,000 pages of municipal records involving the impact of the September 11 attacks on air quality health, as well as the city’s response.

Mamdani announced the documents and an online portal for accessing them on Tuesday. The release comes alongside the settlement of two lawsuits pursued by 9/11 Health Watch, which fought for access to these long-withheld documents.

“For too long, New Yorkers have had to fight for access to records that should have been available to them in the first place,” Mamdani said in a statement.

“The devastating truth is that the suffering did not end once the smoke cleared and the dust settled,” Mamdani also said at a press conference “People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air.”

The tranche of documents offers just a fraction of air quality reports on Ground Zero. But they do include an internal memo where New York City weighed possible liability related to air quality.

The release of these records comes three days before the 25th anniversary of 9/11 – which killed nearly 3,000 people in New York City, Washington and Pennsylvania. The documents provide further evidence that city officials knew air surrounding the twin towers was toxic – but misled the public into thinking it was safe, officials said.

“My colleagues and I who represented Ground Zero and the surrounding communities immediately warned local and federal officials of the health risks posed by toxins in the air at the time,” congressman Jerry Nadler said in a statement.

“Our warnings were not heeded, and now we and the public know that City Hall, led by former Mayor [Rudy] Giuliani, predicted that thousands of responders and community members would face devastating long-term health impacts from these toxins.”

New York City council member Gale Brewer voiced similar sentiments.

“For 25 years, first responders, survivors, families, and people who lived, worked and went to school in lower Manhattan have lived with the health consequences of 9/11 while critical pieces of the City’s own record – HOW they got sick – remained out of reach,” she said in a statement.

The portal, Brewer said, “is a great first step toward giving the public access to that record, one that has been denied them under previous administrations …”

Ben Chevat, executive director of 911 Health Watch, thanked Mamdani for “being the Mayor, after 25 years, who finally begins to answer the question: ‘What did the City know about the dangers from the toxic cloud at Ground Zero and when did it know it?’

“For 25 years, four different Mayoral administrations kept from the public, the U.S. Congress, and the City Council documents showing what the City actually knew about the danger of the toxic chemicals in Lower Manhattan and Western Brooklyn after the World Trade Center collapse, even as City officials continued messaging to the public that the air was ‘safe and acceptable’,” he said in a statement.

articles.title: Ex-NFL star believes Mike McDaniel's 'best decision of his career' was joining Chargers with Justin Herbert
articles.excerpt: Danny Parkins makes his predictions for the 2026/27 NFL Season, including Caleb Williams winning MVP, and the Buffalo Bills and Seattle Seahawks facing off in Super Bowl LXI. Plus, Nick Wright, Chris ...
articles.body_text:
Danny Parkins makes his predictions for the 2026/27 NFL Season, including Caleb Williams winning MVP, and the Buffalo Bills and Seattle Seahawks facing off in Super Bowl LXI. Plus, Nick Wright, Chris Broussard, and Kevin Wildes ask what a successful season would look like for the Los Angeles Chargers and Justin Herbert, and if Maxx Crosby will become a Dallas Cowboy.

While one team in Los Angeles is getting all the recognition throughout the NFL, another is gearing up for what they believe will be a season to watch on their front at SoFi Stadium.

The Los Angeles Chargers sharing a home with the Los Angeles Rams might be hard if you're battling for headlines, but this team has the chance to be just as explosive in 2026.

Why? Mike McDaniel joined Jim Harbaugh's staff in L.A. as the team's new offensive coordinator, and he hasn't shied away from his feelings about his quarterback, Justin Herbert, in the slightest throughout training camp. Simply put, he's obsessed with what Herbert can do, to the point where he's expected to be opening up previously locked plays in his explosive scheme.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSIBLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel and Justin Herbert of the Los Angeles Chargers look on before a preseason game against the San Francisco 49ers at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, Calif., on Aug. 20, 2026. (Getty Images)

Former Chargers star linebacker Shawne Merriman has faith his old squad will be back in the playoffs this season, and McDaniel will be a major reason why they could be contending far beyond just representing the AFC come Wild Card weekend.

"I think Mike McDaniel has made the best decision of his career," Merriman told OutKick in a recent interview. "That’s even outside of leaving the San Francisco 49ers. I think they had something fun, an explosive offense at one time with [Jaylen] Waddle, Tyreek Hill and things like that out in Miami. But he had an opportunity to get a head coaching job at a couple of places, and he didn’t feel it was right.

"So, what happens is you take the best position that puts you back in the driver’s seat after this next year or two so you can go take the job you want."

When McDaniel joined the Chargers, he said he was "geeked" to work with Herbert, whom he believes "hasn't neared the ceiling to what he's capable of." That's saying something considering Herbert has thrown for 5,000 yards in his career, and has proven to be among the top talents in the NFL at quarterback.

CHARGERS QUARTERBACK JUSTIN HERBERT AND POP STAR MADISON BEER ANNOUNCE ENGAGEMENT WITH ROMANTIC POST

But McDaniel's words are something that has Chargers fans geeked, too, especially if there's an extra gear he could unlock with the former first-round pick.

"Justin Herbert had to be the biggest influence of going there, because now you have an explosive quarterback," Merriman added. "He’s an explosive offensive coordinator, so the deep balls down the field, we’ve already seen Quentin Johnston down the field – he’s explosive. You’ve got Ladd McConkey who can work the middle of the field and get open in shorter routes. You have a hell of a running back that comes back healthy this year. …They have an explosive opportunity to win."

Merriman even said that McDaniel joining Harbaugh was interesting at first considering their "quirky" nature in terms of how they coach. But it's been a seamless transition thus far, though Week 1 against the Arizona Cardinals will be the true indicator on just how in sync Harbaugh, McDaniel, Herbert and the rest of the team are.

Offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel of the Los Angeles Chargers warms up before a preseason game against the Los Angeles Rams at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, Calif., on Aug. 27, 2026. (Getty Images)

However, no matter how great the Chargers are in the regular season, a dark cloud hangs over the head of the team, especially Herbert, as he has yet to win a playoff game since entering the NFL.

Merriman was very impressed L.A. was even able to reach the playoffs as the No. 7 seed in the AFC last season considering key injuries to players like tackles Rashawn Slater and Joe Alt, linebacker Khalil Mack, rookie running back Omarion Hampton and more. But Herbert seemed to will the team there, while the defense stepped up big time in key moments down the stretch.

The New England Patriots, though, won 16-3 on Wild Card weekend and Herbert suffered his third career playoff loss. It's something that has to change for the Chargers, but Merriman has an optimistic mindset it will this season.

"Justin Herbert’s going to have that dark cloud over him until he gets deep into the playoffs, right? If he wasn’t so talented, I don’t think the expectations would still be so high. But he has all the tools to do it," he said.

"He’s tough as nails. He had that hand [injury], and he battled through it. I just have so much respect for Justin Herbert."

Offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel of the Los Angeles Chargers shares a laugh with Ladd McConkey during training camp at The Bolt in El Segundo, Calif., on Aug. 11, 2026. (Getty Images)

It will be a daunting road for the Chargers to reach the playoffs in general this season despite having an easier start with the Cardinals and Las Vegas Raiders meeting them at home. The Chargers have arguably the toughest schedule in the league facing stretches that include AFC West foes like the Denver Broncos and Kansas City Chiefs twice, while having to travel to the Buffalo Bills, Seattle Seahawks and Baltimore Ravens. They’ll also have to face those Rams in a SoFi Stadium battle on Nov. 1.

But if there was ever a time to prove McDaniel’s offensive scheme is what was needed to change things for the Chargers, this is the ultimate test for a team and fan base begging to make a run at the Vince Lombardi Trophy.

Scott Thompson is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Sharpeville massacre, 66 years on: Families still wait for justice
articles.excerpt:
Sharpeville, South Africa – Paulina Mathinye was five years old when her father left home for a meeting near the police station in Sharpeville, a township south of Johannesburg.

“I’ll go run to him,”...
articles.body_text:
Sharpeville, South Africa – Paulina Mathinye was five years old when her father left home for a meeting near the police station in Sharpeville, a township south of Johannesburg.

“I’ll go run to him,” Mathinye recalled thinking. “He will pick me up like daddies always do with their beloved daughters.”

On March 21, 1960, Mathinye’s father joined other men from the community at a gathering protesting apartheid’s pass laws, which required Black South Africans to carry documents restricting where they could live and work.

“There was a meeting here at the old police station, so he accompanies those fathers to the meeting. But then he never came back.”

Police opened fire on the protesters that day in what became known as the Sharpeville Massacre.

Apartheid-era police records put the death toll at 69 and the number of injured at 180. Research published in 2024 using police records found that as many as 91 people may have been killed and 238 injured. The higher figures are also cited by lawyers representing Sharpeville survivors and families.

The massacre became a defining moment in South Africa’s struggle against apartheid. March 21 is now commemorated as Human Rights Day, and South Africa’s democratic Constitution was signed in Sharpeville in 1996.

But for the families of those killed and injured, the consequences did not end that day.

More than six decades later, survivors and relatives are seeking redress through the courts.

Lawyers for Human Rights has filed an application in the Gauteng High Court challenging the continued existence of the Indemnity Act 61 of 1961, an apartheid-era law that the applicants say prevented survivors and dependants of those killed from pursuing civil and criminal proceedings arising from the massacre.

The applicants are also seeking certification of a class action involving survivors who were shot and dependants of those killed.

For Mathinye, the legal fight is inseparable from the life that followed her father’s death.

He had been the family’s breadwinner. After he was killed, her mother worked as a domestic worker to support five children.

“We sometimes go to bed with empty stomach. We sometimes go to school and when we come back from school we find nothing to eat.”

There was no electricity, and sometimes her mother could not afford even a candle for the children to study.

“There was no light. There was no library. Struggle even to buy a candle, a mere candle.”

She stayed in school and applied to study further, but her family could not afford it. She eventually began working while still young to help support her mother and siblings.

When she encounters people she went to school with who became teachers and nurses, she thinks about the life she might have had.

“If my father was not shot, maybe I was going to be one of those people… Maybe by this time I would be a teacher.”

Charne Tracey-Mamdoo, a lawyer in the Strategic Litigation Programme at Lawyers for Human Rights, told Al Jazeera that victims and families attempted to pursue claims soon after the massacre.

“Immediately after the Sharpeville massacre, victims and families did attempt to pursue these sorts of claims, but they were barred because in 1961 the apartheid government enacted the Indemnity Act.”

The applicants argue that the Act created a legal barrier to civil and criminal proceedings arising from conduct covered by the legislation.

The current case challenges that barrier.

Lawyers for Human Rights is asking the High Court to declare the Indemnity Act unconstitutional and invalid. It is also seeking certification of a class action for survivors who were shot and dependants of those killed.

The applicants must first persuade the court to grant the constitutional relief they seek and certify the proposed class action. If the case proceeds, individual claims for damages could then be pursued.

More than 70 survivors and relatives have expressed support for or interest in the proposed litigation, according to Lawyers for Human Rights.

Tracey-Mamdoo said lawyers had spent years locating surviving victims and witnesses, reconstructing claims and gathering historical and expert evidence.

The survivors’ age has added urgency. Many of those directly affected by the massacre are now elderly, and some who spent decades seeking redress have died without seeing the matter resolved.

Ishmael Poho was six years old when his father left home for a community meeting on March 21.

“He said, ‘No, I’ll come back. You need to stay home.’”

Poho saw his father again briefly that day.

“That was the last time I saw my father that day.”

It took his mother three days to find his body.

According to Poho’s account, related partly through an interpreter, his mother searched police stations before eventually finding him among bodies that had been placed in garages.

“At that station, there were vehicle garages as part of the building and the infrastructure. However, bodies were piled up or stacked up in those garages,” the interpreter said.

His father’s death changed the family’s circumstances.

His mother had never worked and did not speak English. She eventually found work as a domestic worker in a nearby white neighbourhood. As the children grew older, they also worked to support the household.

Poho, now 72, thinks about the people he went to school with who became teachers, nurses and other health professionals.

“If my father was alive, I would have been different. My life would have been different from the life I have lived.”

For Mauleen Maine, the loss began before she was born.

According to family history passed down by her grandmother, he had returned from a night shift, gone to buy bread and then returned to the meeting.

After his death, Maine’s grandmother struggled financially and eventually sold liquor to survive. She died without seeing the matter resolved.

Maine’s parents later continued seeking redress. They too died without seeing justice.

She told Al Jazeera through an interpreter that compensation alone would not be enough. Her family also wants better housing and educational opportunities for their children.

For families like hers, the question is not only what was lost in 1960, but what might have been different in the decades that followed.

For Vincent Thamae, a member of Voices of Sharpeville who has worked with survivors and families, the case cannot be reduced to compensation.

“It’s not a question of the amount of money. It’s the question of how much does it need for a change in the lives of the victims and survivors?”

Thamae argues that the effects of the massacre reached beyond those who were shot.

“The victims were not only those who were shot,” he said. “We maintain even the whole township was a victim.”

Lawyers for Human Rights says the plaintiffs also want dialogue with the South African government about appropriate reparations and recognition.

The formal court case, however, is narrower. The applicants are challenging the Indemnity Act and seeking relief that would enable the proposed class action to proceed. The court has not yet ruled that the Act is unconstitutional, nor has it determined that the government is liable to compensate the applicants.

That distinction matters because Sharpeville occupies a powerful place in South Africa’s democratic identity.

It is remembered every year as a symbol of the struggle for human rights.

For some of the families who lived through the massacre, however, remembrance has not amounted to redress.

Lawyers for Human Rights says 51 Sharpeville survivors were formally awarded reparations through the Truth and Reconciliation Commission process.

Poho had expected the democratic government to address the concerns of survivors and families.

“We were happy that a Black government had stepped into office, and we were hopeful that our issues would be met and, you know, justice realised, only to realise it became worse. Nothing ever came.”

The government respondents will have an opportunity to respond to the application before the High Court considers the relief sought.

There is no clear timetable for the proceedings.

For Tracey-Mamdoo, the age of the survivors makes the case urgent.

“They’ve already waited a very long time for this to happen and we are doing everything we can to just kind of move that process forward.”

Their fathers died more than six decades ago.

Their families have lived with the consequences ever since.

Children grew up without fathers. Breadwinners were lost. Educational opportunities disappeared. Mothers struggled to keep households afloat. And in some families, the next generation inherited not only the consequences of the massacre but also the fight for redress.

Sharpeville is remembered as a turning point in South Africa’s history.

For these families, the story remains unfinished.

And Mathinye is still asking the question she has carried since she was five.

Authorities announced a major breakthrough in a decades-old cold case, identifying human remains found nearly 49 years...
articles.body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Authorities announced a major breakthrough in a decades-old cold case, identifying human remains found nearly 49 years ago in North Carolina as belonging to a runaway 15-year-old girl who disappeared from Maryland.

The skeletal remains were discovered more than six months after Cindy Marcell Blizzard went missing in the spring of 1977, according to the North Carolina State Bureau of Investigation (SBI).

Authorities said the manner of death remained undetermined, but the case was being investigated as a homicide. They said the remains were found in a wooded area near a Wilson County manufacturing facility roughly five hours south of Blizzard's home.

The "circumstances surrounding the location and recovery of the remains raised the probability of foul play, and the investigators are treating the case as a homicide," the SBI said.

TEEN FOUND IN SHALLOW CALIFORNIA VINEYARD GRAVE IDENTIFIED NEARLY 50 YEARS LATER AS FAMILY WARNS KILLER

Authorities identified human remains found nearly 49 years ago as those of Maryland runaway teen Cindy Marcell Blizzard. (North Carolina State Bureau of Investigation )

According to officials, skeletal remains and clothing were found Dec. 29, 1977, near a Firestone plant that produces vehicle tires.

A medical examiner determined the remains had likely been there for six months to two years and belonged to a white female between 16 and 23 years old.

In the decades that followed, the case went cold as forensic technology was not advanced enough to identify the remains, authorities said.

"For years, investigators compared dental records against missing persons cases without finding a match," the SBI said.

GIRL KNOWN AS 'CHELSEA JANE DOE' ID'D 26 YEARS AFTER MUTILATED BODY FOUND HUNDREDS OF MILES FROM HOME STATE

FILE — A road runs through a wooded area in Asheville, North Carolina. Investigators are pursuing a homicide probe in the case of a missing teen whose remains were found in a wooded area.  (George Rose/Getty Images)

The case was reopened in 2010 by a state anthropologist, who submitted the remains for DNA testing and cross-referenced the results with federal databases, officials said.

However, the investigation did not gain momentum until 2024, when the SBI’s Cold Case Investigative Team reviewed the case again using forensic tools that did not exist in 1977.

WOMAN FOUND IN SHALLOW GRAVE ID’D AFTER 44 YEARS AS MILLIONAIRE TIED TO ESTATE MURDER PLOT

When the case qualified for advanced DNA testing, forensic scientists extracted preserved genetic material from a bone sample, according to the authorities.

"A genealogy service used the profile to trace potential relatives, pointing investigators toward a 15-year-old girl who had run away from Monkton, Maryland, in the spring of 1977," the SBI said.

The identification was made with assistance from the FBI’s NCIC Investigation and Operational Assistance Group, the Maryland Department of State Police Homicide Unit and the Raleigh Police Department’s Intel Unit, authorities said.

FILE — A young doctor conducts research in a laboratory. Forensic teams in North Carolina have identified the skeletal remains found nearly 49 years ago in Wilson County.  (iStock)

Investigators continue to search for answers surrounding Blizzard’s death.

Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

articles.title: Establishment Dem defeats socialist challenger in crucial battleground Senate primary

Rep. Chris Pappas on Tuesday won the Democratic Senate no...
articles.body_text:
Dem Rep. Chris Pappas, in a Fox News Digital interview, pitches himself to New Hampshire’s political middle as a heated Senate primary nears.

Rep. Chris Pappas on Tuesday won the Democratic Senate nomination in swing state New Hampshire, in a key race that is a must-hold for the Democrats in the midterm elections.

Pappas defeated socialist rival and first-time candidate Karishma Manzur, the Associated Press reports, in the showdown to succeed retiring longtime Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the first woman in the nation's history elected governor and senator.

Republicans haven't won a Senate election in New Hampshire in 16 years, but they view the open Democrat-held seat as a top flip opportunity in the fight to hold their slim majority in the midterms.

The race between Pappas and Manzur was one of the final fights in a six-month primary season that saw the far-left score a slew of high-profile victories over centrists in what's been framed as a battle for the Democrats' ideological future.

THESE 12 MIDTERM RACES WILL DECIDE WHICH PARTY CONTROLS THE SENATE

Manzur, who saw a surge in support in recent weeks, took the fight to Pappas.

"All he wants to do is just get his little cushy job and go to D.C. Go to all these parties and these restaurants and just do whatever the bare minimum is," she charged in a Fox News Digital interview.

The first-time candidate, scientist with a Ph.D. in biochemistry, and nonprofit leader who is a member of a local Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) group, pushed for universal health care, raising the minimum wage to at least $20 per hour, abolishing ICE, and ending all military aid to Israel for what she argues is the Israeli government's "genocide" against the Palestinian people in their war against Hamas in Gaza.

Manzur argued that Pappas, who has been supported over the years by the pro-Israel lobby AIPAC, is a "genocide enabler."

"Chris Pappas has had his turn and has not been able to serve this state honorably. He hasn't done a good job in serving his corporate donors, his AIPAC foreign-aligned lobbies," she claimed.

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas of New Hampshire, a U.S. Senate candidate, is joined by Sen. Elizabeth Warren of neighboring Massachusetts, at a campaign stop in Dover, N.H. on Sept. 5, 2026. (Jessica Sonkin/Fox News)

Pappas, in an interview with Fox News Digital, said, "Israel's a historic ally of the United States, the only democracy in the region. And you can say that while you have vehement disagreements with the Netanyahu government as I've expressed."

And referring to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Pappas said, "I think Netanyahu's being incredibly reckless right now. He faces voters in a matter of weeks and could lose his election. And I think that would be important to set a new tone for the U.S.-Israel relationship."

Pappas, who was the frontrunner for his party's nomination ever since Shaheen announced early last year that she wouldn't seek re-election, enjoys strong establishment and union backing. And for over a year, as he runs for the Senate, Pappas also takes aim at what he calls a political system "rigged for billionaires."

Regardless, Manzur charged that Pappas took a page from her playbook.

"It's really embarrassing and insulting to the people of New Hampshire. He's been there for eight years. He has not provided any of that sort of populist messages, and now he's realizing, wait, he's dropping in the polls, and now he has to catch up," Manzur charged. "That's another one of those deceptions that... Chris Pappas always engages in."

CHECK OUT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POLLING IN THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS

Democratic congressional candidate Karishma Manzur speaks with supporters during a campaign stop in Dover, New Hampshire, on Sept. 3, 2026. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

Pappas defended his record, noting "I've been fighting to change Washington to get big money out of our political system since I got elected to Congress in 2018."

And Pappas emphasized he's "appealing to those voters between the 20 and 80-yard line on the political playing field, and there are a lot of them in New Hampshire. This is not a left-wing or a right -wing state. It's a state of voters who are pragmatic."

Pappas will face off in the general election against either former Sen. John E. Sununu or former Sen. Scott Brown.

Asked how he'll unify his party after a primary showdown that turned heated, Pappas said, "I've always been able to bring people together, and that's how you do things in New Hampshire."

Pointing to the high-stakes head, Pappas said, "Democrats are coming together regardless of how these primaries are shaking out because they understand where the real fight is. This is an election here in New Hampshire that's going to determine the balance of power in the United States Senate. And Democrats won't be able to take the majority back in the US Senate if they don't hold this specific seat here in New Hampshire."

Paul Steinhauser covers the national campaign trail from coast to coast for Fox News
